If your pet is young and healthy, the cost of coverage may not seem worth it. But that math can change fast.

Senior Writer & Licensed Insurance Specialist

It feels natural to protect your pet’s health with insurance in the same way you protect your loved ones with health insurance. After all, fur babies are part of the family.

But if you’ve shopped for pet insurance recently, you might have cringed at the cost. Should you really pay hundreds of dollars every year for something you might not use? For some pet parents, the answer is yes, even if their pet is young and healthy. And that’s partly because of how pet insurance handles pre-existing conditions.

A pre-existing condition is any illness or injury that shows symptoms before your pet insurance policy takes effect. Pet insurers usually won’t cover these conditions.

Dr. Rebecca Greenstein, chief veterinarian at Kleinburg Veterinary Hospital and veterinary expert for rover.com, says she’s seeing an increase in claim denials based on pre-existing conditions. “The whole point of insurance is you want broad spectrum coverage for a variety of things,” she says. “By the time they're excluding major organ systems and anything related to that, you may be paying monthly for coverage that doesn't actually help you when you need to go make a claim.”

If you’re considering pet insurance, it’s best to buy a policy before your pet needs it.

Your pet’s pre-existing conditions will determine which treatments and procedures insurers cover down the road.

Say your dog has a history of allergies. If you buy a policy after your four-footed friend has shown symptoms, pet insurers typically won’t pay for allergy shots or other treatments. The exclusion might also apply to related problems like itchiness or ear infections, says Dr. Michael Goldstein, medical director at Billerica Veterinary Hospital and Thrive Pet Healthcare.

He offers the example of a dog who goes to the vet for a hotspot one year and an ear infection the next. If you got pet insurance for your dog between those visits, the insurer might deny your claim because both issues could be caused by underlying allergies.

The best way around this type of scenario is to buy coverage when your pet is young, before any symptoms develop.

» MORE: The best pet insurance for pre-existing conditions

It’s tricky to figure out if pet insurance will actually save you money in the long run. The most common type of plan covers accidents and illness. It costs an average of $836 for dogs and $435 for cats each year, according to the North American Pet Health Insurance Association (NAPHIA). You could pay these premiums for years before an emergency surgery or chronic illness makes its way to your financial doorstep.

It’s impossible to know for sure whether your pet will stay healthy or run up sky-high vet bills. But you can assess the potential value of pet insurance by looking at common chronic conditions that pets develop with age and how much it costs to treat them.

For instance, “cats generally, as younger animals, don't have a lot of problems,” Goldstein says. “But as they get older, there are definitely common issues. Older cats in particular get chronic kidney disease.”

In cats over age 10, the Cornell Feline Health Center estimates that as many as 40% have chronic kidney disease. The annual cost to treat this condition can top $1,200.

Another example is atopic dermatitis from skin allergies, a common ailment affecting as many as 15% of dogs, according to the Cornell Richard P. Riney Canine Health Center. A single vet visit to address these itchy, persistent symptoms can cost $250 or more. And while that’s a fraction of what you might pay for pet insurance, costs of chronic conditions can add up over your pet’s lifetime.

Vet bills can also balloon quickly if chronic conditions require surgery. One example of this is hip dysplasia, a genetic disorder that can cause arthritis and pain in large-breed dogs. Depending on the procedure, you could pay up to $10,000 for hip surgery.

Many pet insurance plans cover treatments for hip dysplasia, including surgical costs, as long as it's not a pre-existing condition. However, some policies have waiting periods of six to 12 months for orthopedic issues like hip dysplasia. If symptoms develop during that waiting period, the condition will be considered pre-existing. That’s another argument for buying your pet’s coverage earlier rather than later.

Most importantly, having insurance means you can choose the best treatment for your pet no matter the cost. “It's really tragic when it's a life and death decision that is needed and it’s based on someone's financial constraints,” Greenstein says. “What is best and what's affordable often are not on the same side of the spectrum.”

One option to keep pet insurance affordable is to buy an accident-only plan. This type of coverage is usually much cheaper, costing about $190 annually for dogs and $112 for cats, according to NAPHIA. These plans cover injuries resulting from accidents, which include not just wounds and broken bones but also objects or toxins your pet might swallow.

However, an accident-only plan won’t help with some of the most common vet expenses. Illnesses, not injuries, are behind most claims submitted to pet insurer Lemonade, the company said in an email. In the past year, more than 60% of Lemonade's pet insurance claims stemmed from illnesses. That’s twice as many as the next-largest claim category, which was preventive care. A similar trend can be found in data from Nationwide, where chronic diseases make up a clear majority of pet insurance claims submitted to the company in 2025.

If you opt for an accident-only plan or no coverage at all, it’s still smart to set aside some savings for those inevitable pet emergencies and illnesses. This pool of funds can keep you from having to make difficult decisions about your pet’s care based solely on the cost of treatment.

#3194. Identity Governance And The Challenge Of AI Agents Moving At Machine Speed

Praerit Garg, CEO, One Identity, trusted leader in identity security, helping enterprises protect and simplify access to digital identities.

​An employee might spend an afternoon retrieving customer records or checking account details. Meanwhile, an AI agent might tick off those tasks within seconds, then repeat them thousands of times without pausing. We’ve reached a golden age of automation, where AI can do more than just automate—it can make decisions and act upon them at speeds that even a whole team of humans could fail to match.

But there’s a catch. While every individual action performed by an AI agent may fall within defined permissions and parameters, all it takes is one excessive entitlement or poorly designed approval process for an AI to cause significant damage. And because AI makes automation much simpler to achieve, allowing employees to turn existing permissions into powerful automated workflows with a single prompt, it’s becoming much harder to govern. With McKinsey reporting that up to 40% of organizations are already scaling an agentic AI system in at least one business function, this is quickly becoming one of the year’s defining security issues.​

Much of the industry’s response has focused on building entirely new identity and governance architectures specifically for AI agents, but they actually already have the right tools at their disposal in the form of identity governance and administration (IGA) and privileged access management (PAM). The same questions that are asked of humans should be asked of machines: Whose authority is the agent exercising? What information can it access? Which actions can it take, and when should additional approval be required? Instead of rebuilding governance architectures from the ground up, businesses simply need to refocus the tools and learnings already at their disposal, particularly zero-trust architectures.​

Microsoft made a significant investment in exploring a more code-centric approach with code access security (CAS) some 25 years ago, but the company later deprecated it and no longer treats CAS as a security boundary because too many paths can allow privileges to be elevated. Microsoft now directs developers toward enforceable operating-system boundaries, including user accounts, which reinforces the idea that creating a specialized control layer doesn’t necessarily provide stronger protection than applying established security boundaries consistently.​

I was recently introduced to an elaborate access governance system designed specifically to stop AI agents from taking actions their users never intended. The organization’s concerns were legitimate, of course, but the solution their team proposed, like Microsoft’s, added so much complexity that they didn’t even consider they may already have the answer.​

An agent acting on someone’s behalf should, at most, only be able to use the permissions granted to that user. If an employee can view a customer record but can’t export an entire database, an agent working for that employee should also have the same limitations applied to it. If the agent can approve a payment or gain access to another business function that the user could not, the first question should be why those permissions were available in the first place.​

The early internet created a similar “trust crisis.” As businesses began distributing software online, users had no easy way to know who had created a program or exactly what it would do once installed. Worms such as Code Red and Nimda showed how quickly malicious code could spread when software was allowed to move and execute across connected systems. That’s when the industry decided that a form of trust infrastructure should be built around digital signatures, certificates and policies, which governed which software was allowed to run.​

Step back into 2026, and the same story is unfolding. Organizations need to establish where an agent and its underlying model came from, authenticate the identity it uses, restrict the systems and data it can reach and require approval before any actions are performed. A trusted model may reduce the risk of deliberately malicious behavior, but identity controls (based on least privileged and zero trust principles) still provide the enforceable boundary when prompts are ambiguous, permissions configurations are flawed or an agent reaches an “unintended” conclusion.​

AI magnifies the consequences of every single entitlement decision. A permission that posed a manageable risk when exercised occasionally by an employee can pose a greater risk when an agent uses it continuously across thousands of tasks. It’s up to humans to assess whether those permissions are still appropriate, what limits should apply and when additional approval is needed. PAM already provides the means to control and audit privileged access according to those decisions, helping organizations put their assessment of business risk into practice.​

Each autonomous service simply needs to have its own identity, a clearly defined supervisor and permissions tied to its specific “role.” In a multi-agent workflow, one agent might retrieve customer data while another updates a business system. Giving both access through the same broad credential would make it difficult to determine which agent performed an action or revoke one agent’s access without disrupting the entire workflow. Existing IGA and PAM capabilities can provide that accountability, provided they’re equipped to govern all identities continuously and revoke access at machine speed.​

AI is new and exciting, but we need to move away from the idea that an agent’s ability to reason about an action gives it the authority to perform it. That decision must remain external to the model and enforceable through the identity infrastructure.​

There’s no escaping the fact that AI agents will become more capable, more autonomous and more deeply embedded in everyday business operations. Every one of those agents must act through an identity, exercise permissions and encounter moments when additional authority is required. As agents become more capable, every organization should be able to explain which permissions were granted, on whose authority and, ultimately, who is accountable for their actions.​

(MLCI -1.98%) executed three strategic transactions during the third quarter to transition its asset management base from legacy noncore vehicles toward scalable permanent capital structures. Management completed the Yieldstreet transaction and the merger of the Alternative Credit Income Fund into BC Partners Lending Corporation, while announcing a pending agreement to manage the AFA Asset Based Lending Fund. The company also reached an operational milestone at its Ability Insurance subsidiary by launching direct origination of multiyear guaranteed annuities following a new credit rating from AM Best. Management reported that these structural changes are intended to improve operating leverage and drive GAAP profitability as the benefits of these initiatives flow through the financials in late 2026 and 2027.

BC Partners held approximately 2% as of that date and is actively working to increase its ownership position. We see that as a further expression of the alignment between our two organizations. Our net loss also continued to improve quarter-over-quarter, and we expect this quarter's results to converge more closely with the true earnings power of our business. We really believe we have built that.

And while alternative asset managers have faced challenges year-to-date, redemption requests at the largest semi-liquid funds are easing, wealth flows are recovering. Mount Logan benefits from a sticky, stable capital base, that allows disciplined deployment and let us hold the line on both risk and returns. We are reviewing corporate overhead, professional expenses and fund-level infrastructure to improve operating leverage. Third, our BDC ecosystem, where we hold economic interest and cash fees from BCP Investment Corporation, BCPL, and where consolidation creates more efficient scaled vehicles and stronger fee economics. Common thread is that we use the capabilities and infrastructure we've already built to attract durable capital and improved operating leverage. Excluding funds withheld and including intercompany elimination of management fees, net investment income for the third quarter of 2026 was $14.2 million an increase of $1.2 million or 9% compared to the second quarter of 2026. This decline reflects the SSL recapture transaction I mentioned earlier, where management agreed to allow SSL to recapture a $70 million block of MYGA liabilities and supporting assets that had previously been reinsured to Ability, in exchange for an upfront recapture fee of $1.9 million. Second, spread-related earnings or SRE, will now exclude net realized gains and losses on the sale of investments. Previously, realized gains and losses were included in SRE.

If you have the Chase Sapphire Reserve® or the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠, here’s what you can expect when you book a vacation home through The Edit:

Up to $250 in statement credits on prepaid stays of two nights or more. Chase Sapphire Reserve® cardholders are capped at $500 in credits a year, while Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ cardholders get up to $1,000 (starting Jan. 1, 2027).

$150 in-stay credit when booking a stay of at least four nights.

Early check-in and late checkout, when available.

Compared to booking hotels and resorts with The Edit, you’re losing out on perks like a $100 property credit (which doesn’t have a four-night minimum), complimentary breakfast and room upgrades.

While cardholders will be able to redeem points toward vacation-home stays, Chase told NerdWallet that these bookings will not be eligible for Points Boost at launch.

You’ll also need to book vacation homes at least seven days in advance — a requirement that’s currently in place with standard vacation homes available in Chase’s travel portal. Chase said it plans to reduce that requirement in the near future.

Chase’s addition of vacation homes to The Edit follows American Express’ recent move to add Airbnb Luxe properties to its own lodging credit for eligible cardholders.

When you book a vacation home for four nights or more through The Edit, you’ll get a $150 in-stay credit to use on services like massages, a private chef, dry cleaning and airport pick-ups.

Options vary by property, but you’ll see a list of available offerings prior to booking your stay. You won’t be able to see pricing, but you can reach out to a Reserve travel designer — a travel concierge who can help plan your trip — to get pricing estimates prior to booking. (You won’t be able to contact the vacation home host until after you’ve booked your stay.)

While it’s nice to get the credit, the four-night minimum could be frustrating for cardholders. When you book hotels through The Edit, there isn’t a stay minimum to get the $100 property credit (although you must stay two nights to use your eligible card’s $250 prepaid stay credit).

By comparison, AmEx offers a $250 Airbnb Experiences credit on the American Express Platinum Card® or The Business Platinum Card® from American Express each calendar year when you book a prepaid Airbnb Luxe property through its travel portal. Terms apply. That statement credit is good for the rest of the calendar year in which the booking is confirmed. However, you can only unlock one $250 credit a year, even if you make multiple bookings.

Booking a vacation home through The Edit makes the most sense for longer group trips.

One of the best perks of booking a vacation home is that everyone gets to stay together in a shared space — something that’s difficult to do in a traditional hotel. If you’re able to get a larger group, you’ll also have more people to split the booking cost with.

Plus, you’ll want to stay at least four nights to benefit from the $150 in-stay credit.

If you’re traveling by yourself or with a partner on a shorter trip, you might find more value staying at a hotel or resort that’s part of The Edit. You’ll get useful perks like complimentary breakfast for two and a $100 property credit.

Ultimately, the biggest benefit of adding vacation homes to The Edit is creating more booking options. If vacation homes fit your travel style, this is a great development to look forward to. If not, you’ll still be able to book hotels through The Edit like before.

Flat-rate travel rewards: Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card

Bonus travel rewards and high-end perks: Chase Sapphire Reserve®

Business travelers: Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card

#3190. Main Street Capital (MAIN) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Record NAV and new SBIC capacity marked a steady quarter for the lender.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Main Street Capital Corporation (MAIN +0.80%) reported third-quarter performance characterized by record net asset value per share and significant capital markets activity that enhanced its liquidity position. Management reported that the company's dual primary investment strategies in lower middle market and private loan segments provided stability despite broad economic uncertainty and increased performance variances among portfolio companies. The company successfully expanded its borrowing capacity through the Small Business Administration and an investment-grade debt offering, resulting in over $1.6 billion in total liquidity to support future investment growth. Management indicated that while lower middle market transaction volume was average during the quarter, the private loan pipeline has increased significantly, positioning the firm for potential expansion in the final quarter of the year.

Operator: Greetings. Welcome to the Main Street Capital Third Quarter Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please note, this conference is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to Zach Vaughan. Thank you, Zach. You may begin.

Zach Vaughan: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us for Main Street Capital Corporation's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today with prepared comments are Dwayne Hyzak, Chief Executive Officer; David Magdol, President and Chief Investment Officer; and Ryan Nelson, Chief Financial Officer. Also participating in the Q&A portion of the call is Nick Meserve, Managing Director and Head of Main Street's Private Credit Investment Group. Main Street issued a press release yesterday afternoon that details the company's third quarter financial and operating results. This document is available on the Investor Relations section of the company's website at mainstcapital.com.

A replay of today's call will be available beginning an hour after the completion of the call and will remain available until November 13. Information on how to access the replay was included in yesterday's release. We also advise you that this conference call is being broadcast live through the Internet and can be accessed on the company's home page. Please note that information reported on this call speaks only as of today, November 6, 2026, and therefore, you are advised that time-sensitive information may no longer be accurate at the time of any replay listening or transcript reading. Today's call will contain forward-looking statements.

Many of these forward-looking statements can be identified by the use of words such as anticipates, believes, expects, intends, will, should, may or similar expressions. These statements are based on management's estimates, assumptions and projections as of the date of this call, and there are no guarantees of future performance. Actual results may differ materially from the results expressed or implied in these statements as a result of risks, uncertainties and other factors, including, but not limited to, the factors set forth in the company's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission, which can be found on the company's website or at sec.gov. Main Street assumes no obligation to update any of these statements unless required by law.

During today's call, management will discuss non-GAAP financial measures, including distributable net investment income, or DNII, and DNII before taxes. DNII is net investment income, or NII, as determined in accordance with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles or GAAP, excluding the impact of non-cash compensation expenses. The DNII before taxes is NII as determined in accordance with GAAP, excluding the impact of non-cash compensation expenses and any tax expenses included in NII.

Management believes that presenting DNII and DNII before taxes and related per share amounts is useful and appropriate supplemental disclosure for analyzing Main Street Capital Corporation's financial performance since non-cash compensation expenses do not result in a net cash impact to Main Street upon settlement and tax expenses included in NII may include excise tax expense, which is not solely attributable to NII and deferred taxes which are not payable in the current period. Please refer to yesterday's press release for a reconciliation of these non-GAAP measures to the most directly comparable GAAP financial measures. Two additional key performance indicators that management will be discussing on this call are net asset value, or NAV, and return on equity, or ROE.

NAV is defined as total assets minus total liabilities and is also reported on a per share basis. Main Street defines ROE as the net increase in net assets resulting from operations divided by the average quarterly NAV. Please note that certain information discussed on this call, including information related to portfolio companies, was derived from third-party sources and has not been independently verified. And now, I'll turn the call over to Main Street's CEO, Dwayne Hyzak.

Dwayne Hyzak: Thanks, Zach. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us. We appreciate your participation in this morning's call. We hope that everyone is doing well. On today's call, we will provide our key quarterly updates, after which, we'll be happy to take your questions. We are pleased with our performance in the third quarter, which resulted in an annualized return on equity of 14.7%, DNII Before taxes per share in line with our guidance from last quarter's call and an increase in NAV per share. We believe that these results continue to demonstrate the sustainable strength of our overall platform, the benefits of our differentiated and diversified investment strategies and the continued strength and quality of our portfolio companies.

We're also pleased to have further enhanced our liquidity position and strengthened our capital structure as a result of an increase in SBIC debenture borrowing capacity through our SBIC funds in the third quarter. And again, through our recent investment-grade debt offering in October, both of which Ryan will discuss in more detail. Given our strong liquidity position and conservative leverage profile, we are very well positioned to continue the growth of our investment portfolio for the foreseeable future, and we're excited about the current opportunities we are seeing.

We remain confident that our unique investment income and value creation drivers, together with our cost-efficient operations and conservative capital structure, allow us to continue to deliver superior results for our shareholders in the future. Our favorable results for the third quarter, combined with our continued positive future outlook, resulted in our most recent dividend announcements, which I will discuss in more detail later. Our NAV per share increased in the quarter primarily due to the impact of significant net fair value appreciation in our lower middle market investment portfolio. Ryan will also discuss our NAV per share increase in more detail.

The continued favorable performance of the majority of our lower middle market portfolio companies resulted in another quarter of meaningful dividend income contributions and net fair value appreciation in our lower middle market equity investments. Consistent with my comments over the last few quarters, we continue to see increased impacts from higher levels of performance variances versus expectations for both our overperforming and underperforming portfolio companies, and those impacts are again reflected in our current results. As a result, we are focused on maintaining a disciplined approach that's consistent with our historical practice to managing our relationships with our overperforming and underperforming portfolio companies.

Overall, based upon our current views of the investment portfolio and feedback from our portfolio company management teams, we continue to maintain a positive view regarding the expected future contributions from our lower middle market portfolio companies. We also continue to see significant interest from potential buyers in several of our lower middle market portfolio companies, which we expect will lead to favorable realizations over the next few quarters. We believe this interest further highlights the strength and quality of our portfolio companies and their exceptional leadership teams. Now turning to our investment activity. The third quarter was slower than our expected normal quarterly activity in both of our primary investment strategies.

Our lower middle market investment activity included 1 new portfolio company investment, which, when combined with other investment activity, resulted in a net decrease in our lower middle market investments of $19 million, while our private loan investment activity resulted in a net decrease in our private loan investments of $2 million. David will discuss our investment activity in more detail. Now turning to our asset management business. We continue to produce positive results for the funds we advise through our External Investment Manager, with the continued favorable performance in the third quarter resulting in meaningful incentive fee income for our asset management business and, together with our recurring base management fees, a significant contribution to our net investment income.

We remain excited about our plans for the external funds that we manage and are optimistic about the future performance of the funds and the expected returns for the investors of each fund. We also continue to be excited about our strategy and expectations for growing our asset management business within our internally managed structure. As part of these efforts, we remain focused on growing the investment portfolio of MSC Income Fund, a publicly traded BDC advised by our External Investment Manager, which is solely focused on our private loan investment strategy with respect to new portfolio company investments.

MSC Income Fund's Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Conference Call will be held later this morning, during which we will provide additional details. Based upon our results for the third quarter and our favorable outlook for the future, earlier this week, our Board declared a supplemental dividend of $0.30 per share payable in December, representing our 21st consecutive quarterly supplemental dividend, and an increase to our regular monthly dividends for the fourth quarter of 2027 to $0.27 per share. These first quarter regular monthly dividends represent a 3.8% increase from the regular monthly dividends paid in the first quarter of 2026.

The supplemental dividend for December is a result of our favorable performance in the third quarter and our net realized gains over the last few years and will result in total supplemental dividends paid during the trailing 12-month period of $1.20 per share, representing an additional 38% paid to our shareholders in excess of our regular monthly dividends. We currently expect to recommend that our Board continue to declare future supplemental dividends to the extent DNII before taxes significantly exceeds our regular monthly dividends paid or we generate meaningful net realized gains, and we maintain a stable to positive NAV per share in future quarters.

Based upon our expectations for continued favorable performance in the fourth quarter, we currently anticipate proposing an additional significant supplemental dividend payable in March 2027. Now turning to our current investment pipeline. As of today, I'd characterize our lower middle market investment pipeline as average. Consistent with our experience in prior periods of broad economic uncertainty, we believe that our ability to provide highly flexible and customized financing solutions to lower middle market companies and their owners and management teams, together with our differentiated long-term to permanent holding periods, represents an even more attractive solution to the needs of many lower middle market companies.

And we are excited about our expectations for the continued growth of our lower middle market investment portfolio. In our private loan investment strategy, we continue to see an improved lending environment, and we have recently experienced a significant increase in the volume of attractive and viable opportunities, which we believe has us well positioned to capitalize on new private loan investment opportunities and to generate growth for our private loan portfolio and our asset management business. And as of today, I would characterize our private loan investment pipeline as well above average. With that, I will turn the call over to David.

David Magdol: Thanks, Dwayne, and good morning, everyone. As Dwayne highlighted in his remarks, we believe that our third quarter financial results continue to demonstrate the strength of Main Street's platform, our differentiated investment approach and our unique operating model. We are pleased to report that the overall operating performance for most of our portfolio companies continues to be positive, which contributed to our third quarter financial results. Each quarter, we try to highlight different key aspects of our investment strategy and differentiated approach that allow us to consistently produce best-in-class results. For today's call, we thought it would be useful to spend some time discussing the support we provide to our lower middle market portfolio companies.

In addition to our ongoing investment management activities and the managerial assistance we offer to our lower middle market portfolio companies, each year, we are excited to host an Annual President's Meeting event for the most senior leaders of our lower middle market portfolio companies. For those of you who are not familiar with our President's Meeting, it's an annual event that we host for our lower middle market portfolio company leaders to network, build relationships, share best practices, learn from each other and from third-party speakers and benefit from being part of Main Street's family of portfolio companies. This year marked the 10th time we have hosted this event.

Based on post-event feedback from our lower middle market portfolio company executives, the event is highly valued by the participants and the event improves each year as we refine our agenda based on the feedback we receive. Topics covered at our most recent event included artificial intelligence use cases presented by a panel of our portfolio company executives, insurance and risk management best practices presented by our in-house Chief Risk Officer. The business case for strategic talent management presented by our in-house talent operating partner, beginning your AI journey presented by a third-party industry expert.

We had an economist speak about his views on the U.S. economy, and our keynote speaker, a Hall of Fame football coach, who shared stories and strategies on leadership, talent development and how to build sustaining winning teams, both on and off the football field. As a result of this annual event, our portfolio companies have increasingly worked together, referred business to each other, utilized each other's operational resources and formed long-term relationships that we believe are invaluable. One important topic we covered this year was best practices for using artificial intelligence in lower middle market businesses.

This session was led by 2 of our portfolio company CEOs, together with the individuals at their companies who lead their internal AI efforts. They presented specific case studies on how they have used AI in their businesses, how they got started, lessons they learned along the way and what they would do differently if they were launching an AI initiative today. The audience Q&A was very active, and we are highly encouraged by the potential benefits our lower middle market portfolio companies can achieve as they continue to adopt AI in the future. Two other important sessions that we had were led by Main Street executives and focused on risk management and human capital at the portfolio company level.

We are pleased to have our Chief Risk Officer present on how we can support our portfolio companies with the implementation of enhanced risk management and insurance-related initiatives that we believe will benefit our companies going forward. Our in-house talent operating partner presented on how we can support our companies as they assess and strengthen their teams, compensation alignment, culture and organizational efficiency. She also addressed succession planning and management, which is a critical area of value creation and risk mitigation for our lower middle market companies.

The engagement from the audience during the event was robust and led to post-event discussions that we believe will ultimately improve the future financial results and operating performance for our lower middle market portfolio companies. Given our primary focus on our lower middle market investment strategy and the unique benefits it can provide to us, our management team partners and their companies, we are excited to bring together the key leadership from our lower middle market portfolio companies at our Annual President's Meeting.

We always leave this event very excited about the quality of the individuals leading our lower middle market portfolio companies and the future value creation that we expect they and their teams can generate for our mutual benefit in the future. We left this year's event more excited than ever. Now turning to the composition of our investment portfolio as of September 30. We continue to maintain a highly diversified portfolio with investments in 187 companies spanning across numerous industries and end markets. Our largest portfolio companies, excluding the External Investment Manager, represented only 3.3% of our total investment income for the trailing 12-month period and 3.4% of our total investment portfolio fair value at quarter end.

Majority of our portfolio investments represented less than 1% of our income and our assets. Our lower middle market investment activity for the third quarter included total investments of approximately $61 million, including an investment of $39 million in a new lower middle market portfolio company, which after aggregate investment activities resulted in a net decrease in our lower middle market portfolio of $19 million. In our private loan strategy, we completed $162 million in total private loan investments, which after aggregate investment activity resulted in a net decrease in our private loan portfolio of $2 million.

At the end of the third quarter, our lower middle market portfolio included investments in 92 companies, representing $3.3 billion of fair value, which was 28% above our related cost basis and our private loan portfolio included investments in 86 companies, representing $2.1 billion at fair value. The total investment portfolio at fair value at quarter end was 117% of our related cost basis. Additional details on our investment portfolio at quarter end are included in the press release that we issued yesterday. With that, I'll turn the call over to Ryan to cover our financial results, capital structure and liquidity position.

Ryan Nelson: Thank you, David. To echo Dwayne's and David's comments, we are pleased with our operating results for the third quarter, which included NII per share and DNII per share amounts that were in line with our prior guidance and another increase in NAV per share. Our total investment income for the third quarter was $142.5 million, increasing by $2.7 million or 1.9% over the third quarter of 2025 and decreasing by $7 million or 4.7% from the second quarter of 2026. Interest income increased by $8.6 million from a year ago and decreased by $800,000 from the second quarter of 2026.

The increase from prior year was principally attributable to the impact of higher levels of income-producing debt investments, partially offset by the negative impact from investments on non-accrual status and a decrease in interest rates primarily resulting from decreases in benchmark index rates on our floating rate debt investments. The decrease from the second quarter was principally attributable to the impact of a decrease in prepayment activity and lower levels of income-producing debt investments, partially offset by an increase in interest income due to an additional day in the third quarter.

Dividend income decreased by $5.7 million when compared to a year ago, after a $1.4 million increase in unusual or non-recurring dividends and decreased by $1.9 million from the second quarter, including a $300,000 decrease in unusual or non-recurring dividends. The decrease in dividend income from prior year is primarily due to a decrease in dividends from our lower middle market companies as a result of exits since the beginning of comparable period in prior year and changes in the performance and capital allocation decisions of our existing lower middle market companies relative to the prior period and decreases from our External Investment Manager, partially offset by an increase in dividend income from our private loan portfolio companies.

The decrease in dividend income from the second quarter is primarily due to decreased dividends from our lower middle market portfolio companies as a result of changes in the performance and capital allocation decisions of our existing lower middle market portfolio companies, partially offset by an increase in dividends from our private loan portfolio companies -- other portfolio companies and the External Investment Manager. Fee income decreased by $100,000 from a year ago and by $4.4 million from the second quarter. The decrease in fee income from the second quarter is primarily due to a decrease in fee income from the refinancing and prepayment of debt investments, lower closing fees and lower middle market investments and other investment activity.

Fee income considered non-recurring increased by $700,000 from a year ago and decreased by $1.9 million from the second quarter of 2026. The third quarter included income considered less consistent or non-recurring in nature, primarily related to dividend, accelerated interest and fee income, which totaled $6.1 million. These income items were $1.8 million or $0.02 per share higher than the third quarter of 2025, $3.4 million or $0.04 per share lower than the second quarter and fairly consistent with the prior 4 quarter average. The increase from the prior year was primarily due to higher non-recurring dividend income and fees. The decrease from the second quarter was primarily due to lower non-recurring fees and accelerated interest income.

Our operating expenses increased by $6.7 million over the third quarter of 2025 and by $1.2 million in the second quarter. The increases in operating expenses from the prior year and second quarter were largely driven by increases in interest expense. The increase in interest expense from a year ago was primarily driven by an increase in average borrowings to fund a portion of the growth of our investment portfolio and an increase in the weighted average interest rate on our unsecured debt obligations resulting from borrowing and refinancing activities, partially offset by a decrease in the weighted average interest rate on our credit facilities resulting from decreases in benchmark index interest rates.

The increase in interest expense from the second quarter was primarily driven by an increase in the weighted average interest rate on our unsecured debt obligations resulting from borrowing and refinancing activities. The ratio of our total operating expenses, excluding interest expense, as a percentage of our average total assets was 1.2% for the quarter on an annualized basis and 1.3% for the trailing 12-month period, and continues to be among the lowest in our industry. Our External Investment Manager contributed $8.4 million to our net investment income during the third quarter, which represents a decrease of $400,000 from the same quarter a year ago and a decrease of $300,000 from the second quarter.

Our External Investment Manager earned gross incentive fees of $3.5 million during the third quarter and waived $600,000 in incentive fees from MSC Income Fund resulting in net incentive fees of $2.9 million. This net result represents a decrease of $1 million in net incentive fees from prior year and a decrease of $100,000 in net incentive fees from the second quarter of 2026. Our External Investment Manager ended the quarter with total assets under management of $1.8 billion. During the quarter, we recorded net fair value appreciation, including net unrealized appreciation and net realized losses on the investment portfolio of $40.9 million.

This increase was primarily driven by net fair value appreciation in our lower middle market and private loan investment portfolios, partially offset by net fair value depreciation in our middle market investment portfolio and fair value depreciation of our External Investment Manager. The net fair value appreciation in our lower middle market portfolio was largely driven by the continued positive performance of certain of our portfolio companies. The net fair value appreciation in our private loan portfolio is primarily driven by net appreciation on several specific portfolio equity investments, partially offset by depreciation primarily associated with increases in market spreads. The net fair value depreciation on our middle market portfolio was primarily driven by net depreciation on specific portfolio investments.

The depreciation of our External Investment Manager was primarily driven by decreases in the valuation multiples of publicly traded peers, which we use as a benchmark for valuation purposes and average incentive fees, partially offset by increased base management fees. Additional details on our net realized fair value activity are included in the press release that we issued yesterday. We ended the third quarter with investments on non-accrual status, comprising 0.9% of the total investment portfolio at fair value and 3.5% at cost.

Net asset value, or NAV, increased by $0.30 per share over the second quarter or 0.9% and by $1.44 per share or 4.4% when compared to a year ago, to a record NAV per share of $34.22 at quarter end. Our regulatory debt-to-equity leverage calculated as total debt, excluding our SBIC debentures divided by NAV was 0.7x, and our regulatory asset coverage was 2.42x. These ratios continue to be more conservative than our long-term target range of 0.8x to 0.9x and 2.25x to 2.1x, respectively. We continue to be active on capital activities, aided by our strong relationships as we continue to manage our overall capital structure diversity.

In September, we received SBA approval to increase our SBIC debenture capacity by $75 million to a total of $425 million with the potential for at least $50 million of additional capacity under current SBA regulations. In October, we issued $500 million of investment grade unsecured notes maturing in January 2030 with a coupon rate of 6.55% and a yield of 6.8%. Given our current liquidity position and recent net investment activity, we were less active in our at-the-market or ATM program, raising net proceeds of $10 million from the equity issuances during the quarter.

After giving effect to our capital activities, we entered the fourth quarter with strong liquidity, including cash and unused capacity under our credit facilities totaling $1.6 billion with our next term debt maturity of $400 million due in June 2027. We continue to believe that our conservative leverage, strong liquidity and continued access to capital are significant strengths that have proven to benefit us historically and have us well positioned for the future, allowing us to continue to execute our attractive investment strategies despite the current market uncertainty. Coming back to our operating results.

DNII before taxes per share for the quarter of $0.98, was $0.09 per share lower than the third quarter of last year and $0.10 per share lower than the second quarter. Looking forward, we expect fourth quarter of 2026 DNII before taxes of at least $0.98 per share with the potential for upside driven by portfolio investment activity during the quarter. With that, I will turn -- I will now turn the call over to the operator so we can take any questions.

Robert Dodd: Congrats on the quarter again. Two questions, both related to pipelines, but the 2 different ones. On the private loan, I mean you characterized it well above average, and I think you said a significant increase in the pipeline. I mean that's quite good. How would you -- and I know when it's early in the pipeline, you don't necessarily know where pricing is going to shake out. That tends to come out at the end, right? And in the past, you've lost some deals at the end related to unacceptable pricing for your return expectations, right?

So can you kind of give us a framework around that in terms of the pipeline being well above average, but I mean do you expect that -- do you believe that market pricing in the private loan market has moved sufficiently that, that pipeline and that would be at sufficient pricing for you to actually be willing to close it, i.e., is that well above average, potentially well above our average originations or just opportunities?

Dwayne Hyzak: Sure, Robert. Good morning, thanks for the question. I'll give you a couple of comments, and I'll let Nick add on anything else that he wants to add. But I would say when you look at our discussion each quarter on pipeline, what we're talking about is transactions that are not finalized clearly. They're still subject to diligence and legal documentation and some other activities. But by the point we put it in the pipeline, I would say the general terms and conditions, size of facility, leverage loan-to-value and pricing are all pretty well defined. Everything that we have that we're quoting here would fit that category. Clearly, still subject to diligence and legal documentation and finalizing the transaction.

But for all intents and purposes, most of the terms have been agreed to. And that's consistent with what we would have been giving to you in the past when we gave commentary on pipeline. Regarding pricing, I think we feel good about the pricing. It will be in line with what you've seen us execute historically. I don't think we've seen significant changes in pricing recently or in terms and conditions. I think overall, we feel good about the nature, types of companies, the transaction structure and pricing that would be in these transactions or investments in the pipeline if they get executed. But that would be my comments, but Nick add on any additional color?

Nicholas Meserve: Yes, Robert. I think the only thing I'd add there would be the pipeline we do quarterly is we kind of do a judgment call on -- consistent judgment call on how that moves forward. And so there's always the risk that either the sponsor doesn't win the transaction end of the day, they don't close or we don't finalize our financing, that's kind of baked into how we view the pipeline and expectations. So there's always a risk that we don't get to the finish line in close. But as of now, we feel really good about the pipeline.

Robert Dodd: And then flipping to the other side, the lower middle market average, average isn't bad. On that, it is an election year. I mean the elections are done, but it was only a couple of days ago, was any of the -- and there's obviously broad economic uncertainty, geopolitical issues with war, et cetera. I mean how would you characterize the likelihood of that lower middle market activity early-stage pipeline or pipeline accelerating given now the elections are behind us, but there's still a lot of other uncertainties.

I mean, just trying to get a gauge on whether there was a temporary lull because of all that, and we could see a reacceleration above average or this is -- well, I mean, average is average. I mean we're going to stay here for a while.

Dwayne Hyzak: Yes, Robert, I would say that it's too early to tell if there's going to be any impact from the election. I think the pipeline is average, as you said, it's not meant to be negative. We want it to be better, obviously. You always want to achieve as much positive outcome as you can, but the pipeline is average. And I don't think it's average because people are waiting on the election. I don't think we expect to see a big change post-election. If there's anything that drives activity to be slower than we would want it to be, I would say it's more just the continued uncertainty in the marketplace.

There's a lot of moving parts and pieces across the U.S. economy, and that can cause transactions to either not come to market or if it does come to market and you get engaged in diligence, you can cause things to not go as planned just because of the uncertainty in the marketplace. But I wouldn't say there's anything that's impacted the pipeline as a result of the recent elections. But David, feel free to add on anything you want to add?

Operator: Our next question is from Arren Cyganovich with Truist Securities.

Arren Cyganovich: Maybe touch on the credit quality side, how are you seeing the health of your portfolio companies, I guess, both on the LMM side and also on the private loan side?

#3189. If Your AI Isn't Working, Fix The Foundation

Merlin Bise is the CTO of Inbenta. He has built conversational AI since before generative AI.

​A lot of the AI deployed into the customer experience over the past three years isn’t performing. That’s just the reality. And the default response I hear, over and over, is to start all over again, evaluating and paying for a new platform.

In most cases, that’s an expensive way to rebuild the same problem.

I’ve been building AI for customer experience since before generative AI showed up. I watched intent matching give way to generative layers, and now we’re into agentic systems that can reason and act on their own. The platforms keep changing. But it isn’t the model that causes the deployment to fail—it’s the knowledge underneath it. I’ve seen that pattern in nearly every underperforming deployment I’ve looked at, going back years.

And look, none of this is a knock on the decision you made three years ago. You made it with the tools that existed then. Those were very different tools.

Here’s what’s new. Fixing the knowledge layer used to be a multiyear, hand-built project. That’s why re-platforming seemed faster, even when it wasn’t. AI now does the heavy lifting up front. It reads, structures and tags your content before anything goes live, so what customers hear is approved, not improvised. Work that used to take a room full of contractors a full year can now get done in weeks, not quarters. If you wrote off your knowledge problem 12 or 18 months ago as too slow or too expensive, it deserves a second look and, honestly, a lot more optimism than it would have earned back then.

Before you run another evaluation, check three things. You can diagnose all of them without a new vendor.

Content written for someone browsing a help site does a different job than content a model has to parse. A model can have the right document and still give the wrong answer. Why? Because two records that aren’t the same can look the same to a system reading them. If a customer asks about one product configuration and gets information about another, that isn’t because the company chose the wrong model or the customer botched the prompt. It’s a structure and authorship problem, and no new platform is going to fix it for you.

Count them. Most organizations have more duplication than they think. As mentioned earlier, a lot of platforms started with intent matching, then added a generative layer later and kept the original intent base underneath. So, now you’ve got two copies of your content, two governance surfaces and two possible answers to the same question. Contact center stacks do the same thing by channel—one store for digital and another for voice. The answer changes depending on which door the customer walked through. If a policy lives in more than one place, you have a consistency problem, not an AI problem.

This is the one that kills deployments. If the subject matter expert who spots a wrong answer has to file a ticket and wait on an engineer, corrections will never keep pace with the business. The person with the knowledge can’t act. The person who can act has no way to judge whether the answer was right. Give that six months, and the system has drifted away from how the company is supposed to operate, without a single error in the logs. You don’t get an alert—you get confused customers.

In the end, you should have one knowledge store instead of several, content structured so a machine can find the right answer and the people who own the policies in control of the answers. And there’s no need to replace your platform.

The economics back this approach up. A full platform replacement is a six-figure commitment before you even count internal time, and moving off an entrenched stack can run several times that. Fixing the knowledge layer costs a fraction of it. And you keep the asset, no matter what you run on top. If you want to switch platforms later, fine. You’ll be moving a structured, governed knowledge base, instead of hauling the same mess to a new vendor and paying them to discover it.

There’s a second-order benefit, too. A consolidated, governed knowledge layer gives you an audit trail. When a regulator asks about a specific conversation, you need to show the question, the answer, the source and who approved it. It doesn’t matter what platform was used. If you can’t see why your AI said something, you can’t defend it.

Here’s my takeaway. Before you run another evaluation, figure out whether you have a platform problem or a foundation problem. Most of the time, it’s the foundation. And it’s more fixable today than it was when you signed that original contract.

#3188. Why Koppers Holdings Stock Flopped on Friday

It missed badly on third-quarter net income.

Investors weren't particularly keen on holding on to Koppers Holdings (KOP -24.39%) stock as the trading week came to an end. The specialty chemical company posted an earnings report that fell short on both the top and bottom lines. With that considerable headwind, Koppers stock closed the day more than 24% down.

Koppers, which specializes in wood preservation and coal-tar distillation chemicals, published its third-quarter figures early Friday morning. The company's sales rose to just over $499 million from the year-ago result of $485 million. Net income not under generally accepted accounting principles (non-GAAP, or adjusted) went in the opposite direction, tumbling to slightly over $15 million ($0.77 per share) from more than $24 million.

Neither headline metric came close to its consensus analyst estimate. On average, pundits tracking Koppers stock anticipated $512 million in sales and an adjusted net profit of $1.34 per share.

The company attributed its improvement in sales to volume increases in both the residential and industrial wood preservative segments. Materials and logistics costs, however, had a significant and negative effect on profitability.

Management is clearly expecting the situation to remain challenging, as it cut several key full-year guidance items. Koppers now expects net sales to come in at roughly $1.9 billion; it previously guided to a range of $1.9 billion to $2 billion. The adjusted earnings per share (EPS) has been adjusted to $3.10 to $3.25 for the year, well down from the preceding $3.80 to $4.20. On a slightly brighter note, free cash flow guidance was raised to $115 million to $135 million; the previous estimate was $110 million to $130 million.

The next few months, and possibly quarters, will be challenging for Koppers, as management recently outlined fresh price hikes taking effect in 2027 to offset sustained higher costs. This surely won't be met with joy by the cost-sensitive railroads, utilities, and wood treatment businesses that buy from Koppers. I'd imagine the company will continue to struggle in such an environment.

#3187. ​The Industrial Revolution Of Intelligence: AI Energy Infrastructure

Bill Wong - AI Research Fellow, Info-Tech Research Group.

​​In my previous article, we examined the emergence of a new data center asset, the AI factory, which is optimized to run AI workloads. Compared to traditional data centers, AI data center campuses require up to 10 times the total facility power capacity, driven by GPU server racks that consume 12 to 28 times more power per rack and thermal density that requires advanced liquid cooling to handle five times the heat generation.

This new industrial revolution is driving an unprecedented demand for power, transforming the utilities industry from a relatively stable and quiet industry to a growth sector.​ Nations and organizations alike will need to optimize their AI energy strategy in order to flourish during and after this revolution.

After reviewing several national AI energy infrastructure strategies around the world, four distinct strategies stand out. These strategies will shape how nations are planning to build the required energy infrastructure for AI workloads.

• Sovereign Regulation-Driven: These jurisdictions introduce legislation to ensure that AI developers must fund their own power requirements, maintain the reliability of the grid and provide the supporting water infrastructure required for these data centers to prevent rising utility costs. In Canada, the country’s recently published AI strategy champions their grid’s 83% investment in clean power. Australia will require data center providers to generate as much energy as they consume. The EU has introduced a sovereign AI compute platform, EuroHPC JU, which aims to “develop innovative energy-efficient HPC software technologies tailored to exascale and post-exascale supercomputers.”

• Market-Driven: These countries rely on the private sector to drive the building of data centers and leverage easily accessible energy resources. The U.S. has begun by reinvesting into nuclear power plants and the use of small modular reactors. The UK has accelerated AI projects through its AI Growth Zones, fast track permits.

• Localization-Driven: Rather than adding additional workloads to the existing energy grids, some countries are locating new data centers near clean energy sources. Japan’s new collaboration strategy leverages nine designated green energy zones. South Korea’s new strategy directs the movement of 18.4 GW of data center workloads out of Seoul to regional nuclear and small modular reactor clusters.

• State-Driven: China’s government is planning to connect renewable energy resources from its western region to its computing hubs in its eastern region.​

In order to assess a nation or organization’s AI energy strategy, one must examine its energy value chain. This involves identifying the source of its energy, determining how power is generated, determining how power is managed and deployed, understanding the nation’s thermal management and understanding the sustainability strategy the nation or organization has implemented.​

Meaningful metrics in this area focus on the total volume, dependability and carbon footprint of the electricity required by the organization in question’s compute infrastructure. Countries and organizations using clean and renewable energy resources will be able to differentiate their energy infrastructure in a positive manner. On the other hand, countries leveraging fossil fuels, like natural gas, may have the short-term benefit of accessing low-cost energy resources, but they will also encounter long-term emissions problems, which expose them to carbon regulation and creates cost volatility.​

Metrics in this area focus on an energy infrastructure’s capacity and its ability to connect, control and optimize high-density energy flow between the bulk electric grid (external) and its computing facilities (internal).

From a macro-grid point of view, which focuses outside of the data center, leaders can use ultra-high-voltage transmission lines, battery storage and AI-driven load-balancing software to absorb the violent swings in demand from GPU clusters, which can dramatically improve power management.

From a micro-grid standpoint, which focuses inside the data center, leaders have a few things to consider. Today’s AI racks demand 130 to 600 kW, and pushing that much power through legacy wiring can generate wasted heat and requires multiple inefficient conversion steps. Modern operators can implement ±400V or 800V DC systems and solid-state transformers to reduce internal heat loss and conversion steps.​

Legacy air cooling can no longer dissipate the heat generated by today’s AI factories. How a company handles this heat is becoming a competitive advantage for any organization running its own sovereign AI infrastructure. I’ve observed some leading operators switching to direct-to-chip liquid cooling in closed-loop systems, which can slash operational water consumption.

Embracing robust environmental stewardship can help nations and organizations keep their data center expansion efforts sustainable, minimizing ecological disruption while preserving critical local environmental resources. Beyond conservation, some advanced operators are turning thermal management into a revenue stream. By establishing facilities in colder climates (like Canada, the Nordics or Hokkaido, Japan) and capturing the 60- to 80-degree Celsius waste heat directly from server racks, those operators can sell that heat to municipal district heating networks.​

Which AI energy infrastructure strategy is the best for a given organization will depend on several factors, and not all options are available for a given country or geographical location, especially those strategies that can leverage a country’s colder climate to reduce cooling costs.

Countries and organizations need to prioritize and align their energy infrastructure architecture with their nation’s sovereign AI strategy. For instance, sustainability initiatives will likely have the best success in countries like Canada and Nordic nations.

Finally, organizations need to learn how to address the current backlash from people regarding AI data centers near their communities. Builders and operators should be prepared to address questions and concerns surrounding the AI energy value chain they’re leveraging, along with its regional costs and benefits. Leaders should focus on sustainability, environmental impact and delivering an accountability framework for the operations of their proposed AI data center.​

During the quarter, we generated approximately $645 million in operating cash flow and made approximately $87 million in upfront payments. Related to El Domo, and Marmato. We also made a quarterly dividend payment of approximately $88 million, and repaid $372 million under our revolving credit facility.

As a result, net debt declined from approximately $1.9 billion at the end of the second quarter to approximately $1.5 billion at the end of the third quarter. Demonstrating the strength of our cash generation and our capacity to rapidly repay debt. At September 30, we had approximately $146 million in cash on hand $1.6 billion of debt outstanding under our term loan, and revolving credit facility. With our revolver nearly repaid, we intend to maintain the term loans to preserve liquidity for potential near term opportunities. While retaining significant flexibility to fund our existing commitments.

Given the strength of our production outlook and high margin business model, we expect to continue to reduce our net debt and return to a net cash position in the near term. While remaining well positioned to pursue additional accretive stream acquisitions. This concludes the financial summary.

TL;DR: Rates fell today, but not by enough to change your mortgage math.

Mortgage rates fell today, possibly helped by post-midterm election clarity and a drop in oil prices.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.01% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is six basis points lower than yesterday and 17 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

As for what’s next: Tomorrow’s jobs report, showing October data, could potentially nudge mortgage rates in either direction. To understand the link between jobs data and mortgage rates, keep reading below the video.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Tomorrow, the Nerds will be watching the release of the October jobs report. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.51% or higher — but there aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

The rate you see advertised is a sample rate — usually for a borrower with perfect credit, making a big down payment, and paying for mortgage points. That won't match every buyer's circumstances.

In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your:

Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles.
