#3184. Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom

Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).

Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.

"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF. "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.

Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly.

Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.

"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."

Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech.

The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.

The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.

Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.

Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).

While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.

Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.

Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.

Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.

Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.

Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb, Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.

Another big winner is 10x Genomics, up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.

On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.

Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.

One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.

It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.

GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.

ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences, Amgen, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, and Moderna.

The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics.

Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."

Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.

Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.

Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.

In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics, a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.

The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.

Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.

Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics.

The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."

Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.

Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.

Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.

T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.

Reinsurance premiums climbed sharply while persistency stayed elevated.

Management reported that elevated persistency, driven by low-rate mortgage portfolios, continues to support the insurance in-force base while purchase volumes remain constrained by housing affordability challenges. The company reported a significant increase in reinsurance premiums as it expands into property and casualty lines, seeking to diversify earnings and optimize capital through synergy credits. Management stated it remains focused on a balanced capital strategy, as evidenced by the authorization of a new $500 million share repurchase program and the maintenance of a quarterly dividend.

You know, I would believe, especially if there is some inflation you could see FHA borrowers migrate to conventional, which I think, again, if that is better for the borrower, that is good. So I think net, it is probably a positive, for the industry, you know, over the next year or 2.

Mihir Bhatia: Got it. The other question I had was just in terms of insurance in force growth at current market size. Right? I mean, if you think about 80% persistency, you have 50%. I guess, ~$50 billion running off each year. And IW is running about that same level. Should we expect insurance in force to be flat or even down next year?

Mark Anthony Casale: Well, it is hard. it is it is tough for me to say right now. I do say that it has been relative flat. I mean, we are entering 2027, kind of the fifth plus year of just a flat market. So-- and I think given where rates were, we were able to grow insurance in force a little bit over the past few years. I would not be surprised if it flattens out a bit. That being said, Mihir, I do think we are levered more for the up when you think about warehousing's been relatively stagnant, and then we can talk all day long about demographics, but I do believe there is a pent up demand for housing.

And kind of the longer this stays, this kind of slowness hangs around, the larger the snapback will be. So look bigger picture, you know, look at a $1.6 trillion of industry, enforced for the, you know, for the whole industry. I would not be surprised to see that grow to $2 trillion. You know, not next year, not but let's say over a certain period of time, again, take our share So I do think growth will resume. And I do not think, you know, and I do not think a lot of investors see that. And that is that is fine. Right? it is hard in this environment.

But I do think we have that kind of growth because housing will come back. It always does. It always resumes. It will grow in line with GDP. You have to think through why it is not growing. And part of it was 2021 was such an anomaly. We literally pulled 5 or 6 years' worth of growth into 1 year. Or 2 years. Home price is up 50% in 2 years. that is just not normal. So now what you are seeing more of the normalization. So we are flattening out.

We are fortunate, as a company that because of the persistent and the benign credit environment, we are still driving a lot of cash flow to the bottom line. But, you know, in some of the other participants, the transaction oriented businesses, it is us. So, but I do think we really. We kind of get-- we kind of look at it internally as we are paid to wait and the way we are kind of managing capital over time. Because remember, insurance in force, it does not grow, the capital needed to support it does not grow.

So that becomes you know, free cash flow, which again, we have used predominantly the last 18-plus months to repurchase shares, which we think that right now is a pretty good use of proceeds, you know, for the Got it.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from Rowland Mayor with RBC Capital Markets. Your line is open.

Rowland Mayor: Mark, I think you said in response to a question that you price for a 2% to 3% claims rate. But then you still book new notices in a much higher figure than that. What would it take to close the gap?

Mark Anthony Casale: Well, remember, when we book new notices, that is not what our ultimate these things roll. So that is our initial claim rate, 2% to 3% roll ins at the end. So it is kind of apples and oranges. So think of it again as the ultimate claim rate. So just picture unit economics. Right? So premium rate, net premium rate, kind of loss rate, which is your claim rate. that is kind of your return on asset. Then you have your expenses and your investment income. it is relatively straightforward, but I do think claim rate for historically for us has been, like, less than 1%. That is just and we are pleased with it.

But I think, normally, you are gonna have to look in that 2% to 3% range. Hence, when you kinda run through the math, that gets you to that 35% to 45% combined ratio. And I do think that is a good guide. 35% to 45% combined ratio, kind of 80-ish percent persistency longer term is actually a good guide as you start to model this stuff out.

Rowland Mayor: Thank you. that is helpful. And then I guess from a competitive dynamic, we have seen a lot of multiyear quota share deals announced in the industry at fairly cheap cost of capital. You expect that to drive any change in pricing decisions as a result of the improved reinsurance dynamics?

Mark Anthony Casale: Great question. I do not know. We do not do I mean, we look at it. We price on an unlevered basis. We do not take the reinsurance cost and rotate that back into the front end. And part of it is just how the market works, right? I mean, there is only 6 participants, so if you use that to lower price, it is easily matched. I would be surprised if the other participants use it that way too because it is it is really just reducing premium in the industry.

So I think what we would do, the way we look at it is we will price for kind of an unlevered return and anything that is, you know, cheaper, so to speak, on the reinsurance side really benefits shareholders. And we took that and just lowered price, and shareholders do not really gain from that. And I think for, you know, reinsurance we generally have gone 2 years. We have seen some of the, we have seen a few participants go 3 years, which again speaks to 1, the demand for reinsurance in MI. there is really not a lot of GSE reinsurance, so we are kind of the only game in town. We like it, and we will.

I think we will continue. We think it is a great tool, but I would remind you that we do like capital too. Alright? I mean, I think reinsurance protects you, in the event of an, you know, kind of a lower, you know, call it higher unemployment, more losses, reinsurance clearly protects you. Capital lets you take advantage of those type of situations. And I give you the example. it is dated now, but in 2020, we talked earlier, we were the lowest in market share. You know? But in 2020, we were. We have only been number 1 in market share twice in our history, and both times were in 2020.

The second and third quarter when we had, we went out and had raised capital in May. We had a lot of capital. We wrote and I think we had a 20% handle on 1, and part of it was because some of the you know, there was not, you know, there was not as much capital around the industry, there is a little bit of a shock event. We took advantage of it. So again, I think you have to look at it both ways. Reinsurance is a great tool. it is really part of our, you know, when we think about buy, manage, distribute as a key piece of it.

But when you think about capital longer term, you also have to worry about the tail. Right? So when we think about how do we think about excess capital clearly insurance in force is not growing, we have a lot of excess capital. Could we use it for you opportunities outside of the core? Relatively small. We would love to plow it back into the core business. And then we look and say, how much do we need in an event? So remember, we hold first loss. We really hedge out against a mezz. You know, we reattach at the top.

So for our business role, and I know you cover the PNC market, a cat event for us is a severe macroeconomic recession. You know, what is the probability of that happening in the next 2 to 5 years? Probably pretty low, not zero. So I think we like, we have been through it. I have managed through the GFC. I have been through the subprime crisis of the late nineties. You know, we have seen the movie before, so we like-- you know, we think having dry powder to take advantage of an event And also when you think about just the, you know, kind of the price of the-- it is a call, Right?

I mean, so the price of holding on to that additional capital, we actually think is relatively cheap. Versus returning all of it to shareholders. I think for us, a capital return, we are gonna be in excess of 100% this year. We bought back 10% of the company last year. Would not be surprised if we are close to that this year. Again, I think we are fortunate in terms of how much capital we are generating. I think we are using most of it to buy back capital, so we think that is the best use of funds now. But we are still we are still retaining a little bit for-- we like to have dry powder.

Either for an opportunity that presents itself on the offensive nature or just being defensive.

Rowland Mayor: And then if I could just sneak in 1 more. We are coming up on 1/1 here Is there any interest in expanding the P&C appetite And can you discuss your premium expectations there?

Mark Anthony Casale: Yeah. I mean, I think we are clearly in conversations now with Lloyd's around kind of our funds at Lloyd's commitments. I think there is a few where we would like to increase our allocation, and there is 1 or 2 we are gonna decline, because, you know, they are-- it is-- they are using a 100% FAL. there is not a lot of alignment. So, you know, we are not the key there is to continue to-- we have talked about testing, we are continuing to test the market. We like our approach with Lloyd's. it is clearly different than some, but I think it is probably more it suits our style.

So you could see us grow a little bit, I would not expect a lot. And then on the, you know, the quota share that we did last year, that actually renews again for another year. And we will look to do potentially do some other retros or even some direct reinsurance with cedents. But, you know, we will see how it goes. We are seeing a lot of the submissions are coming in, but it is really the same unit economics kind of framework that we have, on the MI side. So we are looking at it.

We are we are building out the infrastructure, but I will give you a lot more color in February. it is a little early to tell because we are just starting to see it. But again, lots of capital floating out there. We do not need to kinda push on growth there for the sake of growth.

Rowland Mayor: All right. Thank you for the answers.

Operator: Thank you. A reminder, to ask a question, please press 11 on your telephone. Again, please press 11 to ask a question. Our next question comes from Bose George with KBW. Your line is open.

Bose George: Hey, everyone. Good morning. Actually, just a couple of bookkeeping questions for me. What was the share repurchase activity just in October?

David Bruce Weinstock: Yeah, Bose, it was about $50 million. Not shares. Let me just pull it back up. Yeah, about 51 million for a little over 800 thousand shares.

Bose George: Okay, great. And then actually, in terms of the tax rate, it was up a little bit.

David Bruce Weinstock: You know what? I got it backwards. Let me correct that. I read it backwards. 802 thousand shares for about $51 million, makes more sense.

Bose George: Yes. Okay. Great. Thanks. And then on the tax rate, yeah, no worries. Thank you. On the tax rate, you know, what is a good number going forward? You know, it is up a little bit. Is it know, more flattish, you know, going forward?

Mark Anthony Casale: Yeah. I would-- Hey. I mean, David can kick in, but I would think kinda I would guide a little higher, Bose, I mean, that is kind of 17-ish, maybe even 18-ish percent. Just remember the friction cost we have from getting it from the U.S. to Bermuda. You know, so there is a 5% withholding tax. So you can kind of do the weightings. But I would be a little conservative there if I were you.

Bose George: Okay, great. And then actually just 1 more. The other income line item, just to confirm that is the GSE CRT business. Right?

David Bruce Weinstock: No. Actually, other income for MI, this quarter, which had a little bit of an increase, that would. You know, we have disclosed, we have. We our ILN transactions, there is a little bit of an accounting nuance there where we have an embedded derivative where the literature says we have an embedded derivative in those ILN transactions. We mark them to market every quarter. We did have a transaction terminate in the third quarter which released the liability and ultimately flowed into income. So that is what you are seeing there. We have that disclosed in the financial supplement. Not something you see every quarter at that magnitude, but that is that is really what you are seeing.

Bose George: Okay, great. And so the CRT stuff goes through the regular premium line?

David Bruce Weinstock: The reinsurance? Yeah, yeah, is correct. that is right. Yep.

Mark Anthony Casale: The CRT business in Mark will go through the premium. that is right. Yeah. Okay.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from Rick Shane with JPMorgan. Your line is open.

Richard Shane: Look, we see defaults picking up, and some of that is seasonality, and some of that is cyclicality. I am curious where you guys sort of think we are from a cyclical perspective. And can you give us any characterization of the defaults that emerged during the third quarter so we can think about tiers or risk associated with them?

Mark Anthony Casale: Yeah. Hey, Rick. I still do not-- we do not see really any trends. I mean, the defaults are up, so they are close to 22 thousand. I do-- and we sound like a broken record here, but when the book's 40 months old, these guys have been around for a while, some of them are gonna default a little bit more. The newer book 2023, 2024, 2025 book, I do-- I just think it is not as good as the earlier book.

So you know, you are going to see, as David said, larger loan sizes, so some of it is coming through that in terms of the provision, but we do not really see it, you know, we look all the time, right, you are looking at defaults, and you are looking at it, there is a couple ways you have to look at it clearly by geography. Right? Given where home prices could be up and down. You are looking at by lender. Also have to look at it by servicer.

And that is something you have to be careful-- you know, I think investors have to be cognizant of If there is a downturn, you know, can the servicer actually collect the payments from the borrower? And that is going to be critical. We are not seeing much, and again, I would always tie it back to unemployment. Unemployment, I think it actually ticked down, so it was 4.1%. So as long as the economy stays strong, I would not be surprised to see the book continue to. Maybe to normalize, but we do not see any kind of skeletons in the closet whatsoever.

Richard Shane: Got it. As always, I appreciate the transparency, Mark. Thank you. You are welcome.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question comes from Geoffrey Dunn with Dowling and Partners. Your line is open.

Geoffrey Dunn: Thanks. Good morning. Unit economics are double digit, but when we consider the necessary capital buffer, Mark, do you think MI is a double digit return business in a normalized market?

Mark Anthony Casale: Yes, firmly. I mean, again, do not confuse unit economics with our balance sheet. I would look-- we firmly think it is 12% to 15%. that is our hurdle. Also the hurdle with strategic investments as we put money to work there. it is clearly the hurdle at Essent Re. it is the hurdle at Title, and quite frankly, Title's not hitting that hurdle. Because of where rates are. I think, again, the lag between our unit economics and the business is really just the capital we are holding on the balance sheet. And again, Jeff, we just think that is a relatively cheap option. To hold.

And you know, so it is probably it is probably a couple of points, in terms of excess that we are holding. But, again, given where we are in the market and just our experience, you know, we are we are perfectly comfortable holding that capital. And meanwhile, we are still returning a lot to shareholders.

Geoffrey Dunn: Thanks. Appreciate it. Then I apologize. I got the October buyback, but missed the quarter's buyback in town.

David Bruce Weinstock: Yeah, Jeff. So for the quarter, we repurchased about 1.1 million shares for $74 million That was for the third quarter.

Mark Anthony Casale: Yeah, pretty light in the quarter, Jeff. Do not read too much into it. I think we kinda look at it more on a yearly basis. I think we bought a lot back in the second quarter. And again, I think it is it is public, but I think we bought back 1 million shares at, like, $56 in June. You know, someone just had to dump the shares I think it was the week that Google was raising, their $84 billion and people were looking. So we like to take we like to take advantage of those things. And, again, if you look at bigger picture, you know, we continue to grow book value per share.

We have grown it, whatever, since the IPO, 17% to 18%. The stock looks like a bad EKG in terms of the performance. It goes up, but it is pretty volatile. And I think our view is we like to continue to buy it when it gets, you know, we think cheaper and then probably lighten up a little bit. You know, on the on the other end. So I would not read too much in quarter to quarter.

Operator: Thank you. I am showing no further questions at this time. I would now like to turn it back to management for closing remarks.

Mark Anthony Casale: I would like to thank everyone for joining today. Excellent questions, and have a great weekend.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

#3182. What Does a ‘Blue Wave’ Mean for Mortgage Rates?

Democrats won big in the midterms, but mortgage rates have bigger forces to reckon with.

Mortgage rates fell again this week, extending a gradual slide that began well before Election Day.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage fell 13 basis points to 7.05% APR in the week ending Nov. 5, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

Homebuyers’ budgets are feeling the pinch from high mortgage rates, steep home prices and a shortage of listings. On the campaign trail, candidates from both parties promised to make homeownership more affordable. But solving that problem is like untangling 20 years’ worth of Christmas lights from your attic. Yank on one strand, and three more tighten.

“Jumpstarting the housing market relies on a calmer geopolitical environment and bond market in the short run and more housing supply plus a more dynamic labor market in the long run,” Jake Krimmel, senior economist for Realtor.com, said in an email.

A shift in political power won’t erase those challenges overnight. Here's what's driving mortgage rates right now — and where a Democratic Congress might have some pull.

How that affects mortgage rates: The relief of one less uncertainty is giving rates some breathing room.

Election results have cleared up one big unknown for investors. With Democrats controlling Congress and Republicans holding the White House, markets are bracing for the reality that any major spending bills could face roadblocks.

Political gridlock isn't always popular, but weirdly, investors sometimes welcome it. When a divided government limits new spending, the government may need to borrow less than expected — which could turn down the heat on mortgage rates.

But there’s a catch. That same gridlock could make it harder to pass laws to help bring down housing costs.

How that affects mortgage rates: Heavy borrowing from the government and tech companies adds upward pressure to the bond market, where mortgage rates take their cues.

When the government spends more than it collects in taxes, it borrows the difference by selling Treasury bonds. When there's lots of debt for sale, investors may demand higher returns, called yields. Mortgage rates tend to follow the yield on the 10-year Treasury note.

The new Congress still faces a mountain of government debt. What they choose to do about it can ripple through the economy to affect your monthly mortgage payment.

“Sound fiscal policy, rather than deficit-financed spending and standoffs over budgets and the debt limit, can help keep rates in check,” Andy Winkler, managing director for housing and infrastructure policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said in an email.

Meanwhile, Big Tech companies are borrowing a boatload of money to build AI data centers. To get the cash, they issue corporate bonds, giving investors another place to put their money. More bonds flooding the market can push Treasury yields higher, taking mortgage rates along for the ride.

But how long can the AI building boom last? Voters across party lines pushed back against data centers in the midterms. Even if lawmakers pump the brakes on new construction, a slowdown in tech spending doesn't guarantee cheaper mortgages.

How that affects mortgage rates: Wartime disruptions to global oil supplies can fuel inflation, pushing borrowing costs higher.

The unpopular war in Iran likely added to the voter frustration that helped fuel Democrats' midterm victories. Higher energy costs can hit household budgets in multiple ways: at the pump, through pricier goods that need to be shipped, and through higher interest rates on loans (including mortgages) as inflation heats up.

“A resolution would likely improve oil supply, helping to ease price pressures and potentially providing relief for mortgage rates,” Krimmel said.

A Democratic Congress could push for a different approach to ending the war, but it can't make Iran agree to a deal.

Meanwhile, stubborn inflation from the Iran war has raised the prospect of another Federal Reserve rate hike at its Dec. 8-9 meeting. Futures traders now put the odds of a quarter-point increase at more than 80%, according to CME FedWatch. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but investors anticipate its decisions — so mortgage rates often move before the Fed does.

If buying a home makes sense for your budget now, there's little reason to wait just because Congress changed hands. Buyers can sometimes score lower prices in winter, when sellers are more willing to negotiate. But with today’s mortgage rates hovering above 7%, higher borrowing costs can eat into those savings, so it’s important to compare mortgage lenders to get the best rate.

For longer-term hope, look to the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which became law this summer. This legislation shows lawmakers can, in fact, work together to make meaningful progress on housing affordability.

“Even with divided government, lawmakers and the administration can build on that common ground to further boost housing production, preserve existing affordable homes, and help families struggling with high housing and utility costs,” Winkler said.

But new homes take time to build, and your house hunt doesn't have to follow Congress's calendar. Your homebuying budget and local market conditions matter more than the next political headline.

The right card for you may depend on where you travel, how often, and your level of elite status with Bonvoy.

Two of the popular credit cards in the Marriott Bonvoy portfolio deliver various benefits to their users. The right one for you may depend on your typical travel patterns and history, such as if you already have a high level of elite status with Marriott or you travel only to certain regions.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card and the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card both come with valuable perks, but there are quite a few considerations that are worth a thorough review. Many travelers prefer not to have two cards from the same loyalty program, and these two cards are actually quite different from each other (including being issued by different banks).

Let’s take a look at these two Marriott co-branded cards to see if one may serve your needs over the other.

Here's how the cards stack up on the basics.

Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card

While the “winning” card for some may not apply to everyone, we wanted to analyze the card that provides exceptional benefits for travelers looking for a Marriott card in exchange for the cost of the annual fee. Those new to Marriott will find this to be a solid entry-level card, but it also works for Marriott Bonvoy fans looking for some extra perks without a huge outlay of money for an annual fee. These are the benefits that handed this card the win.

The annual fee on the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card is notably less at $95 compared with $250 on the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card. While the earning rates when using the card to pay for Marriott stays are nearly the same, and both have bonus categories where you can earn multiples of points based on everyday spending, the lower-annual-fee card offers a lot of points earning for its low annual fee.

On top of the lower annual fee, it comes with an automatic annual free night award, Silver Elite status and a fast path to achieve Gold if you use the card often. Add to that an annual $100 in airline credits and DoorDash DashPass membership, and you have more than covered the annual fee without considering the other perks.

The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card card’s $250 annual fee is higher, and its annual free night award requires spending $15,000 in eligible purchases. But the card comes with automatic Gold Elite status and more bonus points earned.

There are other cards (like American Express Platinum Card®) that also include free Gold Elite status with Marriott that can provide decent value for their annual fee (enrollment required). From a pure cash maximization perspective, the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card wins because it provides more bang for your buck.

The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card is the only one of the two cards to include an annual free night award, and it has a lower annual fee. It can be used at properties up to 35,000 points a night. This can render great value and is more than worth the $95 annual fee. Hands down, it is the winner in this category.

If you spend more than $15,000 on the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card in a calendar year, you can unlock a free night certificate valid at up to 50,000 points. This is even more valuable than the included certificate that comes with the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card, but it also requires you to spend more on this card to get it.

It is important to consider the opportunity cost of not putting certain types of spend on other cards where you could be earning greater multiples of points for the same type of spending. Would losing those points be worth the value of a one-night-free certificate? Since Marriott relies on dynamic pricing, which means that points rates for a redemption night can fluctuate regularly, in many cases the value may not reach the level of the missed points opportunity.

While both cards offer decent travel protection benefits, only the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card comes with a flight credit. You can earn up to $100 in statement credits when making purchases directly with airlines by spending $250 on the card before the end of 2026 for a $50 statement credit and another $50 credit by spending $50 before June 30, 2027. That gives another point to the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card Boundless card.

» Learn more: Should I be loyal to a single airline?

If you don’t already have a Marriott co-branded credit card and you want to diversify what’s in your wallet, this could be a great option for big spenders. And if you are looking for one of the fastest paths to high Marriott elite status, this card can help you get there.

Both the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card and Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card cards offer bonus points on spending, but the more expensive annual fee Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card card offers more points on more spending opportunities, including the below:

18.5X points on Marriott Bonvoy property spending (1.5X more than the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card card).

4X points at global restaurants, including U.S. takeout and delivery plus U.S. Supermarkets on up to $15,000 in combined purchases, then 2X points (that’s 1X more than what Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card offers and available on $9,000 more in spending).

1,000 bonus points when staying at a Marriott Bonvoy property.

Depending on how much you spend in these categories, you have the ability to earn more points with this card than the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card, including when you are not traveling. And then when you are, you earn 1,000 Marriott bonus points for each paid, eligible stay booked directly with Marriott. This gives it an edge, even though the annual fee is higher.

» Learn more: Hilton versus Marriott — Which one is right for you?

When you get the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card, you’ll receive 15 elite night credits deposited into your Marriott account. This is on top of the instant Gold Elite status you earn with the card, which normally requires staying 25 nights. To reach the next tier, Platinum, you only need an additional 10 nights to reach its 50-night minimum.

This means not only do you start out at a higher elite tier with Marriott just for having this card, but also you can progress more quickly to Platinum. For frequent travelers, the best value of this card is the opportunity to reach the next status tier faster. And if you wanted to keep going, you would only need 35 more nights to get to Titanium, which is rich with on-property perks like lounge access, welcome gifts and room upgrades.

Earning these nights within a calendar year is not difficult for Marriott loyalists, especially if you hit the jackpot during a promotion that offers double elite nights.

The status perks don’t stop there. Once you hit Marriott’s Titanium status, you can then link your account with United Airlines to earn United’s Premier Silver elite status for more benefits when you fly United, including greater baggage allowance and free extra-legroom economy seats at check-in.

» Learn more: Marriott elite status: what you need to know

Both of these cards provide Marriott Bonvoy points earning and elite status, and they both offer a great way to expedite points earning or receive travel and purchase protections when using the card. But the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless® Credit Card packs a greater punch in its benefits for a lower annual fee. It becomes a great additional card to others you may have (like the American Express Platinum Card®, which has its own impressive travel perk lineup).

If you are a Marriott frequent guest, the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card offers higher-tier Gold status and a faster path to even better tiers for perks. But, it costs more each year and does not offer a free annual night.

Deciding which perks are more important for you, as well as looking at what benefits come from other cards in your wallet, will help you make an informed decision on which of the two best suits your needs.

For rates and fees of the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card, please visit American Express' rates and fees page.

#3178. ​Your AI Governance Stops At The Screen: The Blind Spot In AI-Driven Document Workflows

Corey Ercanbrack is CTO at Vasion, leading the AI-native transformation of a cloud-native platform under FedRAMP High.

A state agency mails benefits notices to citizens, with personal data on the page and legal rights tied to what’s printed. When I asked the administrator responsible for its 30,000 endpoints what governs that output process, he said it runs elsewhere, on infrastructure owned by a different team.​

He wasn’t dodging me. That’s how these environments get built, and it produces a blind spot most leaders inherit rather than create. Information is governed where the data lives. Output is governed where the devices live. Those are two teams with different budgets, reporting lines and definitions of accountability, so the artifact carrying the heaviest legal obligation sits furthest from the controls protecting the information inside it.​

The same split appears across other organizations I work with. Major American cities operating under state public records law must produce any official communication upon request, whatever the medium. Their digital channels are instrumented. Paper isn’t. The specialist responsible for its endpoint estate acknowledged that if he sent a printed memo, someone would still have to find it.​

That gap has been survivable because a person stands in it. The employee who printed the memo knows he printed it, and if a request arrives two years later, someone can ask him. In audit terms, he’s a compensating control: what you document and test when the designed control can’t be implemented. Nobody documented this one. It’s been load-bearing for 30 years without appearing in a control matrix, which is why removing it looks costless.​

Agents remove it. Deloitte’s 2026 “State of AI in the Enterprise” report surveyed 3,235 business and IT leaders across 24 countries. Nearly three in four companies plan to deploy agentic AI within two years, while one in five reports a mature governance model for autonomous agents. Among the capabilities Deloitte names as crucial are audit trails capturing the full chain of agent actions.​

When an instruction comes from a system rather than a person, there may be no human intent to reconstruct later and no awareness that a records obligation was triggered. Unless the workflow was designed to capture that context, automation can generate unaccounted output far faster than the informal human process it replaced. Leaders may be automating away a control they never knew they depended on.

Most AI governance programs are scoped to the application: which model acted, what data it reached, what it was authorized to do and what it produced. That work is necessary, but it is not sufficient, because operational documents don’t stay inside one application.​

I have watched a prior authorization request move from a medical record to paper, to a fax machine, to an insurer and return days later as an email. Each system recorded its portion and completed the step it was designed to handle, but none held the thread connecting them: the only view from which the organization could reconstruct the full event. The application finished its task. The business did not, and governance was scoped to the first while the obligation attaches to the second.​

An IT leader at a global distributor gave me a paperless example. More countries where his company operates now require documents to be deposited with a government authority. The regulation specifies where the document must be sent without specifying how it gets there. Treating the output boundary as a printing problem misses the broader obligation to govern the document throughout its journey.​

If an auditor picked up an AI-generated document tomorrow, what could you prove about it? Four questions help determine the answer.

1. Identity: Who or what produced it? Once a document is printed, exported or faxed, the chain of identity breaks. The artifact no longer shows which agent created it, who initiated the action or where the information came from.​

2. Authorization: Who approved its release? Knowing who generated a document is not the same as knowing whether release was authorized. A finished document proves neither.​

3. Audit: What happened between input and output? An agent extracts information, changes content and generates instructions. Record only the finished document, and you can’t show what it did. The record has to replay what went in, what changed, who acted and where it went.​

4. Retention: Can you find and classify it? Without the first three, you accumulate documents you’re obligated to protect and unable to trace, turning a governance gap into a storage liability.​

Miss one, and you don’t have end-to-end AI governance. Instead, you have a partial record of an action that continued without you. I recommend running these four against a live workflow before expanding agent authority. The gaps you find are the ones an agent will only widen.

The instinct is to connect every system, but these integrations are often fragile and require ongoing maintenance whenever one side changes.

Start with the work instead.​ Pick one operational document this week and follow it from creation to final disposition. Mark every point where somebody prints, exports, faxes, signs, scans or retypes information, and keep going after the data leaves the application. The handoffs are where governance stops without announcing it. Test the four questions at each one. Wherever context breaks, you’ve found the real boundary of your program before an auditor does.​

The workflows that hold up often share one trait: The record was designed before the agent was deployed, rather than reconstructed after someone asked for it. That means someone decided where human review belonged and what needed to be recorded at every step, including the agent’s actions. You can’t deploy first and gather the evidence later. The record has to be created when the action occurs, or it may not exist at all. And the destination is rarely as modern as the agent. I’ve watched sophisticated automation end with a fax because that’s what the recipient accepts.​​

Governance has to follow the information through every handoff. The practical perimeter is everywhere the information goes.​​

#3177. Granite Ridge (GRNT) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Production climbs as the company nears positive free cash flow in 2027.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Granite Ridge Resources, Inc. (GRNT +13.28%) reported a sequential increase in production and earnings, noting an inflection point as the company transitions toward generating positive free cash flow in 2027. Management indicated that 2026 represents the final year of investing ahead of cash flow, with future growth supported by a higher oil weighting and the expiration of lower-priced hedges. The company is expanding its operator partnership model through a new agreement in the Midland Basin and initiated a capital return program that includes both a recurring dividend and a share repurchase authorization. Management reported that the traditional non-operated business continues to generate steady cash flow across six basins, while the partnership platform compounds inventory and growth.

Operator: Good day, ladies and gentlemen, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Granite Ridge Resources third quarter 2026 earnings conference call. At this time, all participants are in a listen only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. To ask a question during the session, you will need to press star-1 on your telephone keypad. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded. At this time, I would like to turn the conference over to Mr. James, Vice President of Investor Relations. Sir, please begin.

Farquharson, our President and Chief Executive Officer, who will review the quarter's results and company strategy. He will then turn the call over to R. Kyle Kettler, our Chief Financial to review our financial results in greater detail. Tyler will then return to provide closing comments before we open the call for questions. We ask that you review the cautionary statement in our earnings release. Granite Ridge disclaims any intention or obligation to update or revise any forward-looking statements. Whether as a result of new information, future events or otherwise. Accordingly, you should not place undue reliance on these statements. These and other risks are described in our press release and our filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Information reconciling these measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures are available in our earnings release on our website. Finally, this call is being recorded.

And a replay and transcript will be available on our website following today's call. With that, I will turn the call over to Tyler.

Tyler S. Farquharson: Thank you, James, and good morning, everyone. Let me start with the most important takeaway. For the last year, we have told you that 2026 is the final year we invest ahead of our cash flow and that 2027 is the turn. This quarter, you can start to see the turn in our numbers. Average daily production grew 8% from the second quarter. Oil volumes grew 16%. Adjusted EBITDAX rose 35% sequentially to $107 million And our cash flow before working capital changes covered our drilling and completion capital for the quarter. We are also taking 3 steps today that reflect where the business is going.

First, our Board has authorized a share repurchase program of up to $35 million Second, we are putting a clear definition of adjusted free cash flow in front of you, along with the order in which we intend to use it. Third, we continue to evaluate our operative partnerships and we are excited to name our third operating partner in the Permian. RedTalon Creek Resources. Kyle will take you through the first 2. Let me start with the quarter and the platform. Third quarter production averaged 34.6 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day 55% of it was oil.

We placed 9.2 net wells online most of them in the Permian, and we ended the quarter with 14.6 net wells in process. The other major driver to our quarter-over-quarter EBITDAX growth was natural gas price realization. Our realized gas price rose from $1.12 per Mcf in the second quarter to $3.46 in the third quarter, as Waha basis recovered. Tyler will walk you through that in detail, because it is a real change in our cash flow. Our operator partnership platform remains the core of our strategy. Strategy. And attracts the majority of our 2026 drilling and completion capital.

The advantage starts with sourcing, Our partners find and assemble acreage to their own leasing, ground game, and operator relationships, so we see opportunities that never reach a marketed process. We provide the capital We underwrite every opportunity to our return thresholds. And we control the pace. That is how we have consistently added inventory for under $2.5 million per net Permian location well below where marketed deals command. Admiral Permian Resources has been the flagship of that platform. Today, we are introducing another partner. RedTalon Creek Resources is a Midland based operator Our partnership with them is focused on the Midland Basin.

The core of the group worked at Jerry Resources, where they drilled, completed, and produced more than 200 horizontal wells between 2014 and 2024. Arete's management has helped build 5 Permian Basin ventures including Bold Energy 1, 2, and 3, and Oxbow Petroleum. And its business development team has executed more than $8 billion of upstream transactions. We are going to take the free ports the same way Admiral does. His land team builds positions through grassroots, leasing, and joint ventures with large overlapping asset managers. We provide the capital and we control what gets drilled and when. Arete spud its first well under our partnership in October and we expect them to run a rig during 2027.

Outside the Permian, have built a non-operator position in the Utica Shale that we are increasingly proud of. We hold about 6.3 thousand net acres, and produce about 3 thousand net BOE per day from our interest in over 100 gross producing wells. We built this position from scratch over the past 2 years, through a high volume of small deals and count these opportunities among the most economic in our portfolio. During the quarter, we closed 20 acquisitions for $19 million adding 8 net locations, an average entry cost of about $2.4 million per net location.

Also, we divested over $20 million of oil and gas properties in the DJ Basin at a 3.8x forward x 12 month EBITDA multiple. While there is been a lot of volatility at the front end of the oil curve, we continue to plan our business around the back of the curve. Every acquisition and every operator partnership well has to clear a full cycle return above 25% at the strip. And in today's backward market, those long dated barrels are priced at $70 or below. We are not going to chase near term prices or pay up for assets based on where the front month is trading.

Instead, we will continue to seek longer dated, development opportunities farther out on the curve. Keep our hedge program disciplined and direct any excess cash to the priorities Tyler will lay out. Stepping back, the plan is working. Our traditional non-op business generates steady cash flow across 6 basins, and our operator partnerships are compounding inventory and growth. Through the first 9 months of the year, our cash flow before capital changes has funded our development capital. Dividends and acquisitions have been funded from the balance sheet but in 2027, that changes. We expect adjusted free cash flow to fund the dividend and the rest of our capital allocation priorities leverage falling as our cash flow grows.

We ended the quarter with $42.7 million of cash $130 million drawn on our revolving credit facility, $341 million of principal on our 8.75% senior unsecured notes. Net debt was $417 million and leverage improved to 1.3x from 1.4x last quarter. Liquidity was $287 million Now, for natural gas. Waha bases held through the quarter and gas sales came in at $30 million up from $9.6 million in the second quarter. Waha recovered from record lows in the second quarter as new Permian takeaway came on. And our realized price tripled. A note on how we report, we use 2 stream reporting.

So NGL revenue is shown in the natural gas revenue line on our financial statements. On that basis, our realized natural gas price went from 38% of Henry Hub in the second quarter to 121% of Henry Hub in the third quarter. We expect continued strength from Waha bases and NGL pricing in the fourth quarter. Higher natural gas pricing helps but our focus remains on growing oil volumes. Our mix moved in that direction this quarter from 51% oil in the second quarter to 54.7% in the third. For the full year, we still expect oil volumes in line with the mid midpoint of our original guidance. Actual gas volumes will come in lower for 2 reasons.

Gas that was shut in during the quarter due to Waha prices in the second quarter, while Waha prices were at their low. And our gas weighted DJ divestiture that closed in September. That nets out to a lower top end on production guidance in our new range of 34 thousand to 35 thousand BOE per day. in a higher oil mix now at 51.5% to 52.5%. We also raised our LOE guidance to $9.25 to $9.75 per BOE and our cash G&A from $28 million to $30 million. For the fourth quarter, we expect higher ore volumes than we did in the third quarter, with oil growing faster than gas.

We also expect development capital expenditures modestly higher as well, accounting for cost inflation which should put us at the high end of our guidance range for 2026. Let me move to adjusted free cash flow. We define adjusted free cash flow as operating cash flow before changes in working capital. Less development capital expenditures. Acquisitions are not included in that number. On that basis, we generated $13.7 million of adjusted free cash flow in the third quarter. We think this definition of adjusted free cash flow will enhance the comparability to our peers and provide a clear framework for how we will use our adjusted free cash flow. Here's how we intend to use it. First, the dividend.

We paid $0.11 dividend per share every quarter since becoming a public company. Second, acquisitions that clear our full cycle return threshold at Strip. And third, opportunistic share repurchases. Our Board authorized a repurchase of up to $35 million of our common stock through year end 2027. The program does not obligate us to buy any shares and may be suspended or discontinued at any time. We will fund the program with adjusted free cash flow and within the limits of our credit agreement and our senior notes. Finally, 2027. The incremental EBITDAX from moderate production growth higher oil volume weight and hedges rolling off, we see 2027 EBITDAX well in excess of the third quarter annualized EBITDAX. With that, I will turn it back over to you, Tyler.

Third, Grey Rock. In August, affiliates of Grey Rock distributed 14 million Granite Ridge shares to the limited partners of Grey Rock Energy Fund III. #3176. Stop Measuring Technology Adoption And Start Measuring What It Changes

Gayathri Kolandaisami | Doctoral Researcher | Human-centered digital and AI transformation in water utilities and critical infrastructure.

A technology investment can succeed on paper but still fail to solve the problem it was meant to solve.

I saw this happen long before the AI era. When I started my technology career in 2005, my job was to build and maintain the software used by my clients. Over time, I learned that building the technology was only part of the equation. We also needed to understand why it was needed and how the work was being done:

1. What problem were we trying to solve, or what improvement did we want in productivity, efficiency or service delivery?

3. What should the ideal process look like?

That way of thinking stayed with me as my career moved from software development into larger digital transformation projects. It left me with a principle I still believe today: Technology needs to work for us. We don’t work for the technology.

I was in a position to observe an organization’s reaction when an AI coding assistant was introduced to its developers. The management had invested in this technology long before I got involved in the organization. However, they hadn’t understood or researched where and how that technology could help the developers, what the benefits of using it would be or whether the tool was apt for their environment. The outcome was a KPI introduced at an organizational level to measure the tool’s adoption. So, a developer was considered to have met this part of their KPI by simply showing that they’d adopted this tool.

This left me asking myself: Had we moved away from measuring the outcomes of the technology to simply measuring its adoption? That’s when I realized that we’d started working for the technology and not the other way around.

Make no mistake—every cell in my body screams technology. I want to develop new technologies that could solve a lot of global challenges. I’m a strong believer in new technologies, and I’m fascinated by how quickly AI is evolving. But I also think that we’re forgetting why we invented these technologies in the first place. Sometimes, we race toward adopting the newest technology without knowing what we were trying to make better.

Technology is a means to solve a problem, improve a process or create a better outcome. The technology itself isn’t the outcome.

I came across a 2025 study published in Management Science. The researchers estimated that using an AI coding assistant increased completed tasks by 26.08%. In contrast, another 2025 study that examined experienced open-source developers working on mature repositories found that developers took 19% longer when using the AI tools that were tested.

The lesson from these studies is that technology doesn’t produce the same result in different environments.​

Organizations can easily measure the wrong outcome.

Take software development, for example. Building new software or making a change to existing software can involve requirements gathering, design, programming, testing, bug fixing and implementation. Let’s say we implemented an AI coding assistant. We may think that this tool could cut programming time substantially. However, that isn’t the whole picture, is it? What happens if the AI-assisted code requires more testing? What if developers spend additional time reviewing and correcting it? What if defects increase, and some of the time saved in programming is consumed later in the process?

If we measure only programming time in this scenario, we may conclude that the technology has been highly successful. However, if we measure the entire journey from requirements to delivery, we may reach a very different conclusion.

The entire process matters when measuring the outcome of the technology. If the problem that the technology is addressing is slow delivery, measure the complete cycle from requirements to release. If the problem is quality, understand defects and rework. If the objective is greater capacity, determine whether the team can actually complete more meaningful work.

The metric should originate from the problem, the context and the process, not simply from the technology.

I prefer piloting the technology before widely adopting it. A pilot isn’t simply an opportunity to prove that a technology works. It’s an opportunity to discover whether it works for your people, your processes and your particular environment.

If employees aren’t using a technology, that should initially be treated as information rather than a performance problem. Perhaps they need training. Perhaps the technology doesn’t fit their workflow. Perhaps it works well for some tasks but not others. Perhaps the existing technology environment, including legacy systems or code, limits its usefulness. Or perhaps it simply isn’t solving a sufficiently important problem.

Adoption is only one part of the story. Technology can also affect employee and customer experience. It may remove repetitive work and allow employees to focus on more meaningful activities, but it may also create additional work when people have to check, correct or validate its output. Some outcomes are tangible, such as time saved, costs reduced, greater capacity or more work completed. Others are harder to quantify, such as employee satisfaction, customer satisfaction, trust and confidence in the service being delivered. They’re still outcomes.

As organizations embrace increasingly powerful technologies, the temptation will be to measure what’s easiest to see: licenses purchased, systems deployed, users onboarded or usage rates. Those numbers have their place, but they don’t answer the most important question: What became better because we introduced the technology?

Always remember: Technology needs to work for us. We don’t work for the technology.

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?
