Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Steven Chubak with Wolfe Research.

Unknown Analyst: This is Annie on for Steven. I wanted to just start with a question regarding the impact of midterms and whether you could speak to how you anticipate the midterms will affect deal activity across different sectors. And any sectors you expect will be more or less impacted?

Robert Brown: Yes, very good question, very timely question. I think for us, if we look at these midterms, and we commented this before. In our market, what really helps drive activity is stability. And in some ways, if you have divided government where there's checks and balances, and you have an executive branch that's one party and Congress and other party, it's very hard for either party to over advance their agenda, and that tends to create a little more stability. So I think just in general, a feeling of stability should be good for activity in the private capital markets. And I don't know if this is going to be the case or not.

But the one thing we have seen drive activity in the past is when there is a feeling that Congress for the government is moving towards increasing capital gains rates. If we start seeing that, you may see some accelerated activity. But I think in general, midterms, don't move the needle much. This was a very, I think, unique midterm in that it was such a one-sided midterm. But I think for us, our hope and our belief is that the stability of a divided government is going to result in more activity. And we've heard others comment on kind of the regulatory environment. Obviously, the regulatory environment right now is very good for transactions.

And I think if you believe that's going to change, maybe you accelerate something. For us, I don't see that element affecting our business as much. And as Eric mentioned, the sweet spot of where we play tends to get less regulatory scrutiny anyway just based on size.

Unknown Analyst: Okay. Great. And then I just wanted to ask a follow-up question regarding tax code Section 162M. It appears this tax change, which goes into effect next year could limit tax reductions by increasing the number of covered employees. So I was hoping you could provide any preliminary guidance as to how impactful this could be to your go-forward tax rate beginning in 2027 versus the current baseline.

Theodore Heidloff: Yes, Annie, it's definitely something we're evaluating for next year. It certainly depends on the compensation environment. As we move forward, there will definitely be some upward pressure on the tax rate, but that's consistent with everybody across the industry. And I think we tend not to have as much revenue concentration across our MD base as perhaps some others. So I think that should be somewhat of a mitigating factor. But you're right, that will create upward pressure as we move forward but a lot of variables there continuing to model it.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of James Yaro with Goldman Sachs.

James Yaro: Rob, are higher interest rates having any meaningful impact on your clients? How are sponsors reacting, if at all? And is it the sharp move upward in rates that has more of an impact versus an absolutely higher level of rates?

Robert Brown: Yes, very good question. I would say to date, we're not seeing it affect our business. In fact, to date probably is helping our capital advisory business, about 30%, 40% of what we're doing there is stressed or distressed. So if a cost of capital can push something into needing more of that work. We're not seeing it affect the M&A business. Eric, you may want to talk about kind of why we think that's the case?

Eric Malchow: James, I would say a couple of things. First of all, there is increasing pressure for private equity to deploy assets. And the margin -- the increase of interest rates on the margin is not impacting a sponsor running hard after an A asset. The opportunity cost of not putting those dollars to work is far greater than -- or putting them to work far greater than not putting more. I think also importantly, the strategic buyers that are coming to our processes and competing in our processes, there's often significant synergies that are outlaying any marginal increase in the cost of capital.

So in theory, you would think that the rise in interest rates would decrease in values, but we're just not seeing it in our marketplace. It is predictable, if it's small in interest rate increase, it's just not going to impact it.

Robert Brown: Yes. James, I think you alluded to something. I think if you have a rapid rise where people don't know where it's going to end, then that gets back to creating instability. It doesn't seem like that the interest rate increase environment that we're in. And we'll continue to monitor it because, obviously, conventional wisdom is a higher cost of capital, lower values. But I think what's driving transaction activity, and we've mentioned this in the comments as well as the questions. We'll continue to monitor it. But right now, we're not overly worried about it.

In fact, there's some thought that the interest rate increase could be the catalyst for some sponsors to maybe mark down some of their businesses that are overvalued and could result in more activity, but that remains to be seen.

James Yaro: Fascinating. Okay. Well, that actually brings me to my second question, which is on valuations opinion part of the business. So hoping you might be able to just talk a little bit about trends there that are not related necessarily just to the market backdrop. The first is the impact of the continued shift to more frequent valuations out of a monthly or daily and how this has evolved over, let's say, the period since the IPO.

And then number two, the impact of some of the newer products that you've built in this business, the senior debt indices and the private market index being the 2 that I'm thinking about and how the growth of those 2 products has gone.

Robert Brown: Yes. Good questions. And in terms of the frequency evaluations, James, we just see that continue. I think when we were on the road show, we quoted that over 30% of our valuations are now done more frequently than quarterly and largely driven by the retail money that's coming in. And when you have to have redemptions on a more frequent basis than quarterly, you need valuations. We're seeing that number has gone up. And I think the last I heard in talking to Brian was it's kind of mid-30s now. So we are seeing that continue. You've got some large asset managers come out and say, we're just going to value everything daily because we want to.

And so part of it is the redemptions. I think part of it is there's just a shift for more transparency. So that trend is continuing. And there's no indication that's going to stop. And also on that point, the question on how do we see the midterm effect and to the extent there are more regulations for this business, regulations tend to be good. So we'll see what plays out there. In terms of the product, as we previously communicated, we, earlier this year, announced the S&P Lincoln Senior debt index. We brought that to market. We signed up contracts.

We continue to feel that this index will become and if it's not already, kind of the benchmark of choice over time. In Q3, we launched the monthly and sub-industry indices for this with a very favorable market reaction. Nobody else is doing that on a monthly basis. So we're still not modeling any of this in a material way into our revenues gains, but we think that this is a product that's a branding element to it, and we think, ultimately, this has the ability to have an impact on earnings.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Devin Ryan with Citizens Bank.

Devin Ryan: I want to come back to the opportunity that you guys highlighted several times around kind of larger fees. I'm just trying to understand what's driving that and kind of mapping this out into the future? I mean I'm curious, is that mainly you just pay off from building relationships over a long period of time. And so Lincoln just getting involved in larger assignments as you kind of win those customers over trust? Or is it about expanded capabilities and so now you're kind of opening up maybe a different part of the market that wasn't there for you before.

And then connected there certain verticals here where you feel like you have more of a right to win at least initially here?

Eric Malchow: Good questions. I would say to you that it's an evolution of our business. And if I go back to my prior comments, which is, we have built a platform over time with one, diversified, but two full-service products and building value for those portfolio companies over their hold periods. Our goal is to serve the entire life cycle of that company and have round trips. So perhaps sell that business when it's $15 million of EBITDA and then $40 million or $50 million of EBITDA and then maybe $100 million or $200 million of EBITDA. And you're seeing that. And to your sector question, there are different maturation levels of our industry groups.

And we had particularly strong success this quarter, for example, in data centers and power and those -- we've got the leading position there. So we're taking advantage of the structural trends in that market. But also the expertise that we have in that market but no different across other groups like services or health care or even technology where we've had multibillion-dollar deals. And it really goes to the long-term investments that we made that are now paying off because of the expertise that we have, the deals that we've done in that space, the value we're adding to the private equity groups and the portfolio of companies that we are tracking. Anything you'd add?

Robert Brown: I would just say none of this is a change in our strategy. None of this is, hey, we have a strategy to go up market. I think both Lincoln, and I think many of our peers, I think our clients are realizing that firms like us, our expertise in M&A, the industry expertise that we've built up over decades the disciplined processes that we run can be really, really effective at all sides of business. So I completely agree with Eric. I think it's just it's advising companies over decades and deals to get deals. And when you've announced larger deals and more complex deals than more of those tend to compete.

So I think it's been a function of a lot of building blocks over a long period of time that have put us in a position to continually advise on better, larger and more complex transactions.

Devin Ryan: Appreciate that great color. And just a model question. I don't think I missed this, but on non-compensation costs, the outlook last quarter, I think you framed for full year growth in the high single digits off of the -- I think the comparable base was $157 million from 2025. The third quarter of $43 million was better than we had modeled. So that would seemingly imply something in the low $50 million range in 4Q, if that's still the right framework. So just checking to see if that's still the right framework and any modeling help would be appreciated.

Theodore Heidloff: Yes, Devin thanks for the question. Yes, we continue to expect high single-digit growth for noncomp on a pro forma basis once you had MarshBerry,. Q4 tends to be a little bit seasonally higher as you work through some of the year-end billing for firms like consultants, things like that and tend to come through in the fourth quarter there. But yes, consistent expectations with high single digits for full year.

Operator: This concludes our question-and-answer session. I would now like to turn the conference back over to Rob Brown for any closing remarks.

Robert Brown: Really just thank you all for the engagement today. And hopefully what came through is that we believe we're well positioned to capitalize on the momentum that we have. And we look forward to updating you on our fourth quarter and full year results early next year.

High-net-worth, if we find these types of Penn Trust or Athena deals, we are always interested in those, although there's a lot of private equity money there. And then as that's really kind of local asset management, right?

80% of flows in markets tend to go to local products. We're the one big multinational that plays a lot in local markets. And so that's an area that can be interesting for us.

Matthew Nicholls: And to be clear on Stoneshield, it was a really, really interesting opportunity for us because on the face of that, it looks like it is just globalizing real estate, but it's actually a very interesting entree into more real assets and infrastructure in Europe. So it includes digital infrastructure, industrial storage, innovation. There's a few very key areas that we have no presence in today that Stoneshield is going to give us.

Jennifer Johnson: And I think it's increased Clarion's exposure in Europe by 3x. So...

Matthew Nicholls: Exactly, yes. So we're now 13% or 14% or something in Europe.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Dan Fannon with Jefferies.

Daniel Fannon: So I wanted to follow-up on your outlook for the alternatives growth. I mean you've obviously had very strong growth recently, but can you maybe unpack what you expect to be the biggest contributors to growth going forward? And also just clarify in those targets does not include any inorganic contribution that may come going forward?

Jennifer Johnson: Yes, that's great. So a couple of things. So this year, the $43.2 billion is across real estate, secondaries, private credit, venture and even some of the Franklin Templeton had done some CLOs and infrastructure themselves on the fixed income side. So everybody has contributed. Of that, about $11 billion is Lexington's flagship fund, which is flagship XI. That is right on track from where they would expect to be. It's a little over half, and they expect that fund to be about the size of Fund X. And so they'll be continuing to fundraise into 2028. The [ 37 ] -- we expect year '27 to be -- 2027 to be about mid-30s.

And the fluctuation there of going higher is really around what the CLO market looks like. This year, the CLO market had quite a few re-ups and resets that are sort of unique at times. It was a really good year for CLOs. There was a lot of demand. So it will just depend about whether the market will have demand there, and that may swing a bit higher. And then -- so we expect '27 to be around mid-30s.

We expect that because obviously, if you do the math, you'll see '28 and '29 are a bit lower, and that's really because you're not -- we're not assuming that we're in the market with any particular flagship fund like Lexington. Now if real estate turns around and there becomes a great demand, there could be something interesting there. I will point out that the $100 billion we have in private credit, 95% of it is floating rate. So for institutions that are -- that want exposure to fixed income are worried about rising rates, private credit with what Benefit Street Partners. And again, they're focused on middle market. So they're not funding the hyperscalers.

They're focused on middle market, that's a great place to be. So those are kind of the swings. So the answer is no organic -- no inorganic. It's all organic in those numbers.

Matthew Nicholls: Yes. If we ever have anything inorganic, we'll just update the presentation.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Craig Siegenthaler with Bank of America.

Craig Siegenthaler: So I hope you're doing well. Congrats on raising the fundraising targets. I had a question on the momentum at Canvas. I was curious, which products have been the biggest drivers recently between direct indexing, long/short tax aware, tax overlays. And I know you launched that new preferred partner program, too. And then also, in the last week, a member of the U.S. Senate Finance Committee actually wrote a letter to the U.S. Treasury, urging them to take a look at long-short tax-aware products. I'm wondering how you think about the risk of tax law changes to Canvas, especially in light of the Blue Sweep this week.

Jennifer Johnson: So I'm going to have Daniel answer on this. I would just say that we've avoided strategies that the Treasury is scrutinizing the 351 exchanges, the box spread, the ETFs that the dividends are avoiding. And so we don't see that as an issue. But actually, the Blue Sweep to the extent that taxes go up, there's going to be continuing more demand for tax loss harvesting and the efficiency at Canvas, but I'll let Daniel talk about the strategies.

Daniel Gamba: So I'll say 2 things. One is our Canvas solution is very differentiated in the marketplace for 2 reasons. One, we are among the few ones that can do much more frequent tax loss harvesting rebalancing. So most of the competitors actually do once a month or once a quarter. We do it intraday. So that leads to better performance. And that's a big differentiating factor of Canvas. The other one that is very differentiating is we are creating Canvas as a platform for advisers. So we combine Canvas. So that goes to your question, it has direct indexing. It also have income through options adjusted, our capabilities that we can give more income through options adjusted.

We also have municipal bonds in the platform. So we can offer also municipal bonds in the platform. We also offer as you referred to the P3 model, which is basically third-party fundamental equity tax optimization as well as our own fundamental managed tax optimization within the same platform. So that's a very differentiating feature. We have started to do a long/short as well. So long/short for us is really still very, I will say, very early stage. So the majority has been direct indexing as well as third-party and our own fundamental equities tax optimization.

We expect that to continue to be a big driving force as well as, of course, our strength on distribution that we have, which we added this year alone 118 new partners and RIA teams -- so now the total number of teams is 336. So the momentum is very high because as we build all these new teams, each of them have a lot of more tax loss harvesting that they want. And that's actually what gives us a lot of conviction that the platform will continue to grow Canvas.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Alex Bond with KBW.

Alexander Bond: Just quickly, I wanted to ask around the magnitude of catch-up fees in the quarter and also the margin guide for fiscal '27 incorporates any assumptions around further catch-up fees? And then also on the expense side, I think you mentioned $210 million of cost saves in the trailing year. Can you just speak to the scale of the expected savings in fiscal '27 relative to that $210 million? Just trying to think about how the savings and the ultimate level of reinvestments in the business might compare on a year-over-year basis.

Matthew Nicholls: Yes. So the catch-up fees for the quarter were $18 million, approximately $18 million. For the year, it's $44 million. So on the EFR, the $18 million represents something like $0.3 million, something like that. But as I said, if you look at it over the year, if you take into account retro fees, take those out, PFR year-over-year was 37.4 in both years, and we expect that to be similar in 2027, as I've explained. In terms of the savings, 2027, right now, we're estimating that to be around $75 million, something like that. But it's a little bit of a target that goes up and down depending on the metric. Jenny always says, what's the net amount?

What's the net amount? It's not just about the gross savings. But right now, we've earmarked around that level. And the reinvestment is at least that significant, I would say. So yes, we're very optimistic of areas as we talked about at the beginning, where we can lever that saving amount where we need to in order to reinvest more and save more as needed. So we are confident in our target that we gave you for the year.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Michael Cyprys with Morgan Stanley.

Michael Cyprys: I wanted to ask about private markets in the wealth channel. You've seen success with your platform of evergreen strategies, nearly $10 billion. I was hoping you could speak to the steps that you're taking to accelerate growth from there into fiscal '27, where you're most optimistic on seeing meaningful growth from here? Maybe speak to some of the opportunities around models. And just more broadly, how are you thinking about evolving cost of distribution into the wealth channel for private market strategies?

Jennifer Johnson: Yes. So I mean, I think Daniel covered some of this in there. But today, I think we've added 62 -- in 2026, we added 62 distributors to being able to distribute our wealth products and a lot of interest in Asia. That has probably been a big surprise for us is how much interest in Asia. And we have -- I just came back from Hong Kong, where in 2027, we will celebrate 40 years in Hong Kong. I was in the UAE. We're celebrating 30 years in the UAE. These are markets that the retail wealth channel knows our brand really, really well.

And so we have built out a huge force already in our expense numbers with 100 people who are just there supporting distribution with expertise on the wealth channel. In the wealth channel, sales is hand-to-hand combat. It's each adviser. It's not only getting on the platform, it's each adviser. So we've already experienced a lot of that expense. Now it's about getting on those platforms. And as I mentioned, we've added 62 of them, and we have great vehicles to be sold there. We have at least 6-plus evergreen products, of which I think 3 are over $1 billion. I don't know, Daniel, what else you want to add?

Daniel Gamba: I'll add that innovation is a big driver on this space, Michael. We have new evergreens also coming in infrastructure, multi-asset evergreens. So that's clearly an area that is growing. The other one is we just had the closing of our first CFO collateralized fund obligation this past quarter, $1.5 billion that actually covered retail, VA and insurance companies. And also, as you mentioned, the partnership with Corastone on model portfolios, we are in advanced conversations to try to have it up and running and having this in model portfolios.

And finally, I will say also on the target date, we added privates into our target dates between 3% and 8% across different evergreens, and that's already having like early results in terms of momentum. So I think on the product side, a lot of momentum. I did mention also the success of 34% fundraising coming from outside the U.S. And I will also double down. Europe was also good and Latin America had like great success for us. And a lot of this is just newly appointed or new distribution outlets that will start to pay off in '27.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Brian Bedell with Deutsche Bank.

Brian Bedell: Maybe just in context of the 5-year plan, but also more just futuristic thinking, you guys have been so forward thinking on tokenization and digital assets. Jenny, how does the sort of long term or your long-term view on tokenization in asset classes outside of money market funds? How does that influence or I guess, what part of the 5-year growth plan would be considered attributable to that? Or would that be upside to the plan? And then just also your house views on equity tokenization with the SEC innovation exemption how the fundamental teams are thinking about that? And if I could throw one more product in there, and that would be a company KPI event contracts.

That's obviously a new emerging asset class that has good potential within institutional investment. Maybe any early thoughts on if you would adopt those in the fundamental strategy?

Jennifer Johnson: Yes. So here's what I'd say, Brian. Why is tokenization? Why are we bullish on it? It is a really good programming language that does create huge efficiencies in our business and will enable innovation. And so again -- and I've talked about this before, when we did the -- when the SEC approved our tokenized money market fund, we had to parallel process our old recordkeeping transfer agency system with the blockchain system, and we were astonished by the difference in cost savings. And so that's why we're really bullish that the rails of financial services will ultimately be on chain.

We actually -- we don't differentiate it out in our 5-year plan as far as tokenization as a category. So for example, today, we have tokenized ETFs on the crypto exchanges. If you just take the top 5 crypto exchanges, they have 1 billion wallets. It's slow adoption there. Most people are there, they're buying crypto products, but we are getting some adoption there. As other mainstream players add wallets, then these types of products can go. I think it depends on how important the 24/7 trading is. I do think we'll get to a world where that will be more and more important.

Both of the exchanges are struggling because you have this reality of 2 different rails, the old rails, which are based on batch systems, people have to upload and reconciliation and the new rails. And then can you -- let me just ask clarity on the KPI company. Are you talking prediction markets? Is that where you're going? And if yes, then let me just say, look, we actually think the prediction markets information is interesting. And we have a partnership with Kalshi. We talked to Kalshi and get some of that data. We're not investors in the prediction markets, meaning we don't invest in whatever the bet is on that particular thing.

But we leverage that data, particularly into our systematic models just because it gives you a view of what the kind of individual consumer is thinking. And so tokenization probably will be -- again, the technology is such with the smart contracts that it can be a really efficient way to use it, but they -- it will evolve over time. So long answer to that, we don't have any particular numbers broken out in the 5-year plan on digital assets.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Patrick Davitt with Autonomous Research.

Patrick Davitt: There continues to be a lot of announced revenue sharing changes at the largest wealth platforms. Could you update us on to what extent you expect those changes to impact you? Why or why not? Secondly, remind us how you report those revenue sharing expenses? Is it net of fee rate or in the expenses? And finally, to what extent are those changes baked into your fee rate and/or expense growth guidance?

Jennifer Johnson: Yes. I mean, look, rev share is the nature of our business. It's something we've negotiated and navigated for 50 years. So we will continue to do so, and it's no surprise that as the world has been shifting from mutual funds to ETFs, since the platforms are interested in having some sort of revenue share because they do a certain amount of servicing of those clients. Matt, on the -- what I would say is we've been in these discussions for several years now. So there's nothing -- I mean, maybe it's something that's become more aware with you guys, but it's baked into our numbers. So the way we are today is how you would see it.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Ben Budish with Barclays.

Benjamin Budish: I wanted to just ask about the performance fee expectation for next quarter. I think typically, you guide -- when you talk about your cost to $50 million per quarter sort of as a baseline, it sounds like you're expecting that to be a little bit better. Anything kind of different going on crystallization from any of your alt products? Is there anything else we should read too for the rest of fiscal '27? Or is that commentary really just specific to the next quarter?

Matthew Nicholls: I'd just say there's more activity around our venture capital group that's invested in some of the...

Jennifer Johnson: You may have noted some high profile...

Matthew Nicholls: Some prominent investment that everyone is aware of. So we're invested in a number of those companies. So yes, you'll see some higher performance fees in the next several quarters, and we'll obviously call those out as we get our guidance.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Mike Brown with UBS.

Michael Brown: You guys have talked a little bit about the alternatives platform here. And the fundraising backdrop for the industry still remains a bit tight, but clearly, you've been outpacing your growth. So your products are really resonating in the market here. But you did raise your target by 50%. And so I just wanted to maybe hear a little bit more about some of the building blocks beyond 2027 that kind of support the confidence to raise that target here? And maybe just give a little bit of color on what you're seeing in that pipeline and some of the underlying demand there.

Jennifer Johnson: Yes. So I mean, again, we probably have the broadest breadth of capability in the private markets of any asset manager out there. And so when you just look at the fundraising that we've done so far, not only I already mentioned, it's real estate, it's secondaries, it's private credit, it's venture. But probably more interesting is it's 30 different strategies, right? So this is a very diverse capability that has distribution coming globally. And so that's what's given us more confidence the stuff is resonating. Secondaries, I do think that probably rising rates are going to have an impact on the private equity market. But actually, secondaries can go in and buy based on today's rates.

And so a lot of people who want exposure to private equity are actually preferring secondaries. You get -- you have no J curve, you get a much more diverse portfolio. It's getting repriced right now essentially as no buying books. And so that's been a really strong area in what has been a little bit more anemic fundraising on the private equity side. As I mentioned on private credit, 95% is floating rate. If you're worried about where rates are, it's a great place to be. And the economy still remains very strong.

And so if you've got a fixed income allocation and you can withstand the illiquidity, you're getting a premium in the private credit market and you're getting protection against rising rates. The one area -- and Ventures venture, we've seen that there's -- and so much time is spent on the AI infrastructure and not enough time is spent on all the other incredible innovation that is happening between material science, biologics, new drug pipelines, 3D printing, there's a ton of technology out there that makes the venture really, really interesting. And so again, as an active manager looking in that space, you may say these things are overpriced. I like some of this other stuff.

And so we think venture will continue to have good demand. And then real estate, it kind of depends on where you are. You can see it being slower if you're doing development because people worry about the higher rates. But if you are a landlord, which Clarion is in places, rates often rise with inflation. So it could be a really good income source as well as inflation hedge. So that's what's given us confidence that we'll hit those new numbers.

Daniel Gamba: I will add that the One Franklin Templeton approach to selling, especially institutionally, is also giving us much more white space. Jenny mentioned the 10% of institutions just having one capability from Franklin. So clearly, there's a lot of opportunity. The teams are coming together. So they're offering that across the organization. And results are starting to show like our fundraising like quarter-over-quarter went doubled actually over the past 2 quarters on the institutional space across -- in this case, across all products. But there's a lot of opportunity on the private side to continue to do that.

And we've added also resources in Asia Pacific with other resources in Asia Pacific, with other resources in insurance and in other segments that we were not covering before as proactively. So clearly, that will add more to the confidence on the fundraising that we put in front of you.

Operator: And we have reached the end -- concludes today's Q&A session. I would now like to hand the call back over to Jenny Johnson, Franklin's CEO, for final comments.

Jennifer Johnson: Well, thank you, everybody, for joining the call today. And once again, I want to thank our employees around the world for their continued dedication and service to our clients, and we look forward to speaking to you next quarter. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. This concludes today's conference call. You may now disconnect.

#3164. The United Explorer Card Is Great if You Fly Basic Economy

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

Basic economy tickets come with plenty of restrictions, but holding the right credit card is my top trick for avoiding some of them.

As airfares remain high, that basic economy fare might look more tempting than ever. Saving $100 on a round-trip domestic flight could mean more money for hotels, dining or other experiences at your destination.

I’ve flown my fair share of basic economy flights, which come with restrictions like being unable to select a seat, earning no award miles and boarding last. You also can’t make changes or cancel your itinerary without paying a hefty fee, and — specific to United Airlines — you can’t bring a full-size carry-on on board.

But as a United frequent flyer, I have a secret to share with you: Holding the United℠ Explorer Card (annual fee: $0 intro for the first year, then $150) lets you avoid several of those basic economy restrictions.

Right now, new United℠ Explorer Card applicants can receive this welcome offer: Earn 70,000 bonus miles after you spend $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months your account is open. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles when you add an authorized user in the first 3 months your account is open.

Most major airlines no longer let you earn points or miles on basic economy fares. United is an exception, though — assuming you hold the right credit card.

Eligible cardholders, including those who have the United℠ Explorer Card, earn at least 3 miles per $1 spent on United basic economy tickets, excluding taxes and select fees. That’s half of what a standard economy ticket earns for cardholders (6 miles per $1), but it’s better than zero. If you have elite status, you’ll earn more.

Those miles are in addition to the 3 miles per $1 you earn on all United purchases when using your United℠ Explorer Card.

With the card, your miles can become more valuable. That’s because cardholders get at least 10% off award tickets that are operated by United or United Express. If you have United status, that discount gets bumped up to at least 15% off.

With the credit card, you have access to priority boarding in Group 2. That means you’ll be able to board earlier compared to the rest of the basic economy passengers in Group 6, making it more likely you’ll find space for your carry-on bag.

Now, you might be thinking: Wait a minute… Basic economy doesn’t allow you to bring a carry-on bag. Let me explain how that works.

United enforces its full-size carry-on restriction based on your boarding group. Group 6 passengers can't bring a full-size carry-on.

Because the credit card gets you Group 2 boarding, you essentially skip that restriction.

Premier members — who board in Group 2 or earlier — are also exempt from the full-size carry-on restriction when flying basic economy.

If you don’t want to deal with the hassle of a carry-on bag, you can opt to check it instead.

As long as you pay for your ticket using your United℠ Explorer Card, you’ll be able to check your first bag — and your companion’s first bag — for free when traveling on United. (If you’re booking an award ticket, make sure to use your card to pay for the taxes and fees.)

Keep in mind that if the first flight on your itinerary is operated by another airline, that airline’s baggage rules would apply and you would have to pay for your bag.

Of course, holding the right United credit card only gets you so far.

With basic economy, you’ll still need to pay a fee to change or cancel your ticket, and you won’t be able to select a seat for free.

Ultimately, whether basic economy is a good deal depends on a few factors.

If your plans might change, pay up for standard economy. Otherwise, the penalty to change or cancel will end up costing you more than you saved.

Another thing to consider is whether you’re willing to sit in a middle seat. You might be fine with it for a few hours, but what about a long-haul flight to Asia? Everyone’s threshold is different, so you’ll need to decide whether the middle-seat gamble is worth it.

If your plans are firm and you don’t mind a potential middle seat, booking a basic economy ticket can be a solid way to save money. Just book with a United card like, the United℠ Explorer Card, to avoid the biggest downsides.

#3162. Why The Same Threat Means Different Things To Different Companies

Anuj Goel is CEO and co-founder of Cyware, a company focused on intelligence-led cybersecurity and operational resilience.

Every threat intelligence feed shares a blind spot: It knows the threat but nothing about our specific environment.

The feed carries threat data; only our environment provides context. The industry has spent a decade refining data when it should have focused on environment-specific context.

As a practitioner, the hardest conversations were never about explaining suspicious activity. They were about explaining why it reached us when the best intelligence available had already flagged it. We had the indicators. We just weren’t connecting them to the assets they might reach. What surprised me then, and still does, is that the problem was never a shortage of intelligence or its accuracy. It was the missing step between knowing about a threat and knowing, in real time, that it applied to us. That experience shaped how I think about this space, and it is why I believe context, not volume, is where the real work is.

Intelligence has no universal version; “good intelligence” depends on sector and geography, not sheer volume.

Financial institutions require fraud-focused reporting, while industrial operators need OT intelligence built around controllers and plant-floor realities. Neither is “better,” but they aren’t interchangeable. Relevance is inherently specific to who we are and where we operate.

No feed can see inside our walls, and that’s where we decide which known threats matter to our environment.

Relevance is derived from the assets we actually run. The identities and access paths that connect them. What is business-critical versus incidental? Where our controls are strong and where they are thin. This is the ground truth every external indicator has to be measured against. An indicator evaluated against our environment becomes elevated to a prioritized, actionable risk. The same indicator, without an environment behind it, is just a rumor about someone else’s network.

Relevance is the product of the two: the intelligence our sector trusts, correlated with the infrastructure, data and assets we have. Neither input alone produces it. The best feeds in the world, unmeasured against our environment, cannot tell us what to do first on Monday morning. A perfect map of our environment, with no sector intelligence flowing into it, has nothing to act on either.

Consider when identical intelligence arrives at two different organizations.

For one, the indicator maps to a critical, internet-facing application reachable by elevated identities. This context resolves to a high-urgency risk, requiring immediate isolation and escalation.

For the second, the same indicator maps to a decommissioned service or a segment with existing controls. This context resolves to a low-urgency risk requiring only logging.

Same feed. Same indicator. Same morning. Two entirely different answers, and two entirely different actions determined by adding the context.

This is what customer-specific context means in practice. It is not a cleaner presentation of the same data. It is a different computed result for every organization, because the inputs on the other side of the equation differ for every organization. It determines not only whether to act, but what action is warranted, in what order and with how much confidence. Any system that skips this step applies one global severity score to environments that share almost nothing in common.

One line is worth drawing sharply, because the industry constantly blurs it. Tagging an indicator as malicious is enrichment, attaching a known attribute to a piece of data. Knowing that the same indicator belongs to a campaign actively targeting our sector, that a machine on our finance team touched it three days ago and that the identity behind that machine is exposed, that is context. Enrichment adds metadata. Context fuels risk reduction.

This is also why dozens of feeds never added up to an answer. More raw indicators, unmeasured against our environment, is a larger pile to triage, not a clearer picture. Most security leaders have a graveyard of unused subscriptions to prove it.

Increasingly, the systems making security decisions are not human analysts reading a feed. They are platforms and agents consuming intelligence to prioritize, correlate and act, and a decision engine is only as good as what we put into it.

Feed a system raw, one-size-fits-all intelligence and it inherits the problem we started with: It cannot tell a live risk from an irrelevant one, because the feed never carried that distinction. The input has to be measured against that specific environment, already resolved into what is relevant, exposed and worth acting on.

This reframes what “having threat intelligence” should mean. A feed is not the same as threat context, and a raw feed piped into a decision-making tool does not become context on arrival. Intelligence has to be made relevant before it becomes an input, per sector, per environment, per organization or every tool consuming it is reasoning from a rumor.

The organizations—and increasingly, the systems—best positioned for what is coming are not the ones holding the most feeds. Instead, the organizations receiving actionable context are those that understand what threat intelligence means for them and are equipped to drive necessary security actions.​​

#3161. Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital

Investing giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Co., according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The deal is expected to be announced later Monday morning, they said. Financial terms were not immediately known.

The transaction is significant on multiple fronts. It further advances Apollo's ambitions in Abu Dhabi often called the "capital of capital." The firm has spent the past 15 years building key strategic relationships there, with both the country's investment arm and its core leadership.

Apollo already has a multibillion-dollar partnership with Mubadala Investment Co., first established in 2022 and extended two years ago. At the time of that extension, Apollo said the agreement would strengthen the firm's Capital Solutions platform by enabling the firms to jointly source and provide customized debt and equity financing to companies worldwide.

In 2023, the institutions formed a $2.5 billion joint venture designed specifically to co-invest in global private credit opportunities over a five-year horizon.

For Mubadala Capital specifically — the region's only large-scale asset manager, advising and administering more than $755 billion in assets — the deal further advances its growth strategy under the direction of CEO Hani Barhoush, and its relevance on the global investing stage. It also marks an inflection point for the company's core alternatives business, which has grown to more than $60 billion.

John Zito, co-president of Apollo's Asset Management arm, and Barhoush have worked closely together over the past several years and, according to sources, their close-knit relationship and the success of prior partnerships led to talks of deepening ties. So did the belief that scale in the asset management business matters more than ever.

"Capital as a moat is a big thing," said one person familiar with the deal.

Importantly, the deal also continues a notable shift in the relationship between American investment firms and the Middle East. While the region, and Abu Dhabi specifically, has long been a sought-after source of capital, this deal further reverses that dynamic, with Apollo making a significant direct investment in the country and its investment vision.

Mubadala Capital's international offices include London, New York, Rio de Janeiro and San Francisco.

Apollo's investment in Mubadala Capital is similar to deals the firm has done with other asset management platforms, including Diameter Capital, Thoreau, Motive Partners and others.

Spokespersons for both firms declined to comment.

Investors were reacting to what they considered a lackluster third quarter.

For the period, Essent's total revenue rose by nearly 20% year over year to more than $374 million. That was on the back of a 25% improvement in net premiums written, to almost $303 million. However, the company's foundational business didn't look so impressive, as new mortgage insurance written dipped to $12.1 billion from $12.2 billion in the third quarter of 2025.

Increased provisioning for losses and the expenses connected to them dinged profitability. Essent also saw a 40% increase in other underwriting and operating expenses. This wasn't surprising, as the company's mortgage default rate rose to 2.75% from the previous quarter's 2.5%, and the under 2.3% of third quarter 2025.

Mortgages matter for Essent stockholders, and I believe it's the consistently climbing default rate that's giving them serious pause. I feel they're hungry to see some stabilization, at which point they’ll likely become more bullish on the company's future.

#3156. We Write About Saving Money; Here’s How We Trick Our Brains Into Doing It

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Even personal finance writers and editors need psychological hacks to save money. Here are the tips we use, and why they work.

While staring at the Container Store cart on my phone at 11 p.m., I did something for the first time that I’d read about a hundred times. Instead of spending $200 on more organizational boxes that I categorically did not need, I transferred that amount to my savings account.

Normally, my willpower is no match for the very real psychological phenomenon called present bias: Our brains light up more when we’re rewarding our current selves than our future selves.

Research has also shown that you imagine your future self almost like a stranger — it’s tougher to care about that stranger than about who you are right now. But that night, I saw near-future-me using that $200 on next summer’s vacation. I wanted the vacation more than the boxes. So I abandoned my cart.

I had managed to use a psychological savings trick: Find a goal that helps you envision your future self. With this epiphany in mind, I asked some of my fellow Nerds to share the savings habits they’ve put to work in their own lives. Perhaps reading these can give late-night you some saving inspiration.

Kimberly Palmer, senior writer and spokesperson: I let nonessential items sit in my online shopping cart for at least 24 hours before buying them. It definitely makes me realize I don't need a lot of them! I also informed my children of this rule, and it has helped cut down on their requests — or at least they know they have to be patient.

Karen Gaudette Brewer, head of content: Fellow let-it-sit-in-the-cart person here. I wait for notifications that something's at least 30% off before I make any moves. Ideally, 40% to 50% off.

Julie Myhre-Nunes, managing editor: When I browse online, I add an item to my shopping cart and wait 24 to 48 hours. After that, I either decide it’s a waste of money/an impulse purchase and delete it from my cart (or forget about the cart altogether), or I decide I want it and make the purchase — it’s the former 99% of the time.

Why it works: “Waiting 1 to 2 days allows me to take the emotion out of purchasing. I no longer succumb to marketing or sales, and instead make spending decisions based on what my family and I actually need or can use.” — Julie again, eloquently making the point for me.

Caitlin Constantine, managing editor: My one real shopping weakness is books, and I’ve found I can get a very close approximation of that feeling without spending an outrageous amount of money by going to the library, wandering around the stacks to see what books might look interesting, and checking out a bunch of them. Even if I don’t end up reading them, I’m still helping the library with circulation numbers, so I see it as a win-win.

Spencer Tierney, senior writer: Plus one to Caitlin Constantine’s “my one real shopping weakness is books.” If I want an older or smaller book, I'll try to find it at one of four libraries I belong to on Libby, the library e-book reader app. (The Libby waitlist for new books can take months, so I have to account for that.)

Why it works: There’s no secret here: It’s nice to get free stuff. You might be surprised what the library has to offer, like movies, magazine subscriptions, games, classes and theater tickets.

Pamela de la Fuente, managing editor: We always tell people to automate savings, and I do in my high-yield savings account, but Dasha Kennedy, the woman behind “The Broke Black Girl”, told Elizabeth Ayoola on the Smart Money podcast that you should invest, even a little bit every week or so, for future you. So I just set up a small recurring deposit to my robo-advisor.

Why it works: You only have to make this decision once for your future self, not over and over again. And if you do it early enough, you could avoid being part of the 41% of Americans who wish they had started investing earlier, according to a 2026 NerdWallet survey.

Athena Cocoves, managing editor: To cut down on food delivery, I started cooking when I feel like it instead of when I’m supposed to. I exercise free will and make soup at 10 p.m. It sounds more obvious than it feels, and it's made a big difference in my budget. And it'd make an even bigger difference if I wasn't also rewarding myself with fancy spices and vinegars, but a girl's gotta splurge somehow.

Ryan Brady, lead writer: My wife takes advantage of a T-Mobile freebie that gives us a discount for DoorDash deliveries. She uses it to buy groceries from Aldi instead of takeout. Aldi is far from us. Publix is right across the street, but more expensive. So this saves us money on the actual items and also helps us not impulse buy (as we often do when we're in-store shopping).

Why it works: You don’t need to call on willpower if you can avoid the situation that tempts you to spend money.

» Read more: Strategies to save on groceries that actually work

Kenley Young, managing editor: I use credit cards for most purchases to get those sweet, sweet rewards, but there's a lot in this article that I've also taken to heart.

I've started using library resources more, and it's saving me money on things like monthly subscriptions.

I've negotiated down several monthly bills, too: refinanced my car loan, got cheaper homeowners insurance, opted for a little less auto coverage in exchange for a lower premium, and haggled online with everyone from Xfinity and SiriusXM to my local newspaper until they all gave me a discount.

Plus, I've opted for some home improvement projects with the expectation that my utility bills would be lower. A plumber finally fixed our toilet, which has led to lower water bills, and I even installed solar panels.

Lastly, my analog skill (playing live music) has become a steady side hustle. I play eight to 10 gigs a month, where (on top of my baseline rate) I also get tips, free food and beer.

Why it works: Because you’re Kenley and you put in a lot of effort.

But you don’t need to be Kenley to find a savings habit that works for your personality, your financial situation and even your musical talents. You just need to experiment. Pick the strategy that speaks to you most, and test it out. Which one are you going to try first?

#3151. Cerebras Systems vs. Nebius: Which Artificial Intelligence Stock Is a Better Buy Going into 2027?

Cerebras bets on giant wafer-scale chips while Nebius sells a full-lifecycle AI cloud, but one valuation gap and a cash flow twist could tip the 2027 verdict.

As demand for artificial intelligence reshapes the global economy, choosing between hardware innovators and cloud infrastructure providers is a difficult task. Is Cerebras Systems (CBRS +9.75%) or Nebius Group (NBIS +7.58%) the better buy?

Cerebras Systems focuses on massive wafer-scale processors to accelerate AI model training, while Nebius provides a cloud platform specifically designed for the AI lifecycle. Both companies are scaling rapidly to capture market share in the booming AI sector, but they approach the opportunity from different angles within the technology stack.

Cerebras Systems designs specialized artificial intelligence computing systems built around its massive wafer-scale chips. By manufacturing a single processor that covers nearly an entire silicon wafer, the company aims to provide significantly more speed for AI inference and training, giving it a competitive advantage among semiconductor stocks. As organizations prioritize speed, Cerebras Systems delivers its technology through hardware sales and cloud service offerings to global clients.

In its latest annual report, filed for its 2025 fiscal year (FY), revenue reached nearly $510.0 million, representing a growth rate of 75.7% over the prior year. This rapid expansion helped the company achieve a net income of $237.8 million, resulting in a net margin of 46.6%. This performance marks a significant improvement from the previous fiscal year, when the company reported a substantial net loss of $481.6 million, suggesting a turnaround as adoption of its chips increases.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was -0.5x, meaning total liabilities exceed shareholder equity. The current ratio, measuring the ability to cover short-term obligations, was 2.1x. Free cash flow, which is cash from operations minus capital expenditures, was a negative $392.8 million for the fiscal period.

Nebius Group operates as an AI cloud company, providing a unified platform that handles the entire lifecycle of data and model training. The company targets diverse industries such as healthcare, financial services, and media, offering computing infrastructure for production runtime and deployment. As organizations look for specialized hardware and cloud resources, Nebius positions itself as a primary provider for physical AI and robotics start-ups globally.

In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2025, the company saw its revenue climb to $529.8 million, which was a massive increase of 479% compared to the previous year. This explosive top-line growth translated into a net income of $82.5 million and a net margin of 15.6%. The company has successfully shifted from a period of heavy losses to positive net income as its cloud platform gains traction.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 1.1x, while the current ratio was 3.1x. Free cash flow, calculated as cash from operations minus capital expenditures, was a negative $3.7 billion. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented 21.6% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Cerebras Systems faces significant risks related to the intense competition in the high-performance computing market. The company must continue to innovate rapidly to maintain its performance edge over established giants with vastly larger research budgets. Furthermore, its reliance on a unique wafer-scale architecture creates technical and manufacturing complexities that could lead to potential supply chain disruptions if production yields do not meet expectations.

Nebius Group operates in a capital-intensive industry where building and maintaining data centers requires massive ongoing investment. The company competes against the largest cloud providers in the world, many of whom have deeper enterprise relationships and broader service portfolios. Additionally, the rapid pace of change in artificial intelligence software could make current platform offerings obsolete if the company fails to adapt to new model architectures.

Nebius Group appears more attractively priced because its Forward P/E, which compares the price to future earnings estimates, and its P/S ratio, measuring price against sales over the past twelve months, are lower than those of Cerebras Systems.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Deciding between Cerebras Systems and Nebius Group to gain exposure to the AI sector is a challenge, since each has unique strengths and weaknesses. While I like both companies, my pick to buy is Cerebras Systems.

Cerebras' proprietary wafer-scale chip technology makes it stand out against a sea of semiconductor competitors. Rivals produce smaller wafers and link them together with wires and cables. This creates bottlenecks for AI systems. By producing one giant wafer, Cerebras eliminates this slowdown, making its product superior for AI data processing.

Competition creates smaller wafers because manufacturing defects are inevitable. Throwing away defective small wafers is not as costly as a single one the size that Cerebras produces, which would amount to a multi-million dollar loss per wafer. Cerebras has created a closely-guarded manufacturing and defect management process that avoids the need to discard defective wafers, circumventing the issue.

Validation of its product came when Cerebras partnered with OpenAI in a deal valued at over $20 billion. Now, Cerebras must continue to gain customers, which it appears to be doing. On Oct. 27, the company announced Oracle as a client. I think it can gain more customers going into 2027. That's why I bought the stock.

#3150. Closing The Enterprise AI Security Gap: From Blind Spots To Stronger Defenses

Vasanth Mudavatu, Senior Principal Software Engineer at a Fortune 50 company, dedicated to the security of generative AI and ML systems.

Enterprise AI security is no longer just about preventing inaccurate answers. It’s about preventing an automated system from using legitimate access to expose confidential information or execute unauthorized actions.

EchoLeak, which was disclosed in June 2025, was a Microsoft 365 Copilot vulnerability that allowed a crafted email to trigger data exfiltration without requiring the victim to click a malicious link. Microsoft assigned it a CVSS severity score of 9.3, while NIST separately rated it 7.5.

Microsoft patched the vulnerability, and no evidence of exploitation in the wild was reported. This was a demonstrated vulnerability rather than a confirmed breach, but it exposed a consequential failure: External content could influence a system operating with access to internal information.

If an AI agent put customer data, revenue or reputation at risk today, could your organization explain what happened and stop it before the damage spread? The answer depends less on reassuring model behavior than on enforceable boundaries.

The framework below connects four activities: assessing six security blind spots, prioritizing findings, implementing controls in phases and verifying that those controls work.

Attackers can automate reconnaissance, credential harvesting and data extraction. Enterprises need to examine both how AI can be attacked and how it can accelerate attacks.

Being aware of the following six blind spots turn that concern into an actionable security assessment:

A downloaded model shouldn’t become a trusted production asset simply because it comes from a familiar repository. Modified weights, backdoor triggers and unsafe model-file deserialization are areas requiring scrutiny.

Recommended controls include verifying artifact signatures and hashes, documenting provenance, scanning inbound files and testing model behavior before deployment. Integrity verification establishes whether an artifact matches an approved baseline; behavioral testing examines whether it performs as expected. Neither replaces the other.

Disabling an agent isn’t necessarily the same as removing its access. Credentials, active tokens and downstream permissions may remain usable.

Agents need distinct identities, least-privilege access and short-lived credentials, and revocation workflows should be tested. Assessment should also consider combined permissions across tools, as individually acceptable capabilities may collectively create an unacceptable access path.

A useful operational test is straightforward: Disable an agent and verify that its downstream actions actually stop.

Inspecting the final response covers only one potential exit point. Sensitive information may also appear in tool-call arguments, logs, traces or data written to vector stores.

Monitor these boundaries, restrict outbound destinations and correlate activity across requests. That correlation matters because information can leave in small fragments rather than one easily detected transfer.

The assessment should follow the complete data journey, not just the conversation visible to the user.

The security boundary includes more than the model. Build workflows, libraries, containers and deployment dependencies also require review.

Scan inbound model artifacts, pin third-party GitHub Actions to specific commit hashes and maintain an AI-specific inventory of model and software dependencies. These measures help teams identify what they deployed and investigate compromised components.

The objective is traceability, knowing which artifacts and dependencies support each production capability.

A compromised agent may use legitimate tools and credentials to interact with connected systems. Shared memory and agent-to-agent communication introduce additional paths through which malicious instructions can propagate.

Organizations should authenticate communication, verify message integrity, inspect memory and implement per-agent quarantine. Additionally, review Model Context Protocol tool metadata for adversarial instructions or unapproved changes.

Trust should be established at each boundary rather than inherited automatically from another agent.

An agent inventory must capture more than a name. Security teams need ownership, approved capabilities, authorization context and a defined retirement process.

Automate discovery, log audits at the action level and decommission workflows that revoke credentials, address retained memory and preserve required audit records. These controls connect governance decisions to what agents do.

A gap analysis becomes useful when it drives priorities. Evaluate risks using likelihood, impact, difficulty of detection and an exposure multiplier for multi-agent environments.

Treat the resulting score as a prioritization aid, not an objective prediction. Organizations should document their assumptions and calibrate escalation thresholds to their own systems and business consequences.

• The missing control and supporting evidence.

• The test that will demonstrate closure.

Don’t consider a control complete merely because a policy or configuration exists. Closure should require evidence that it works.

The roadmap begins with agent discovery, model integrity checks, outbound monitoring, pipeline hardening and kill-switch implementation. Subsequent phases introduce managed identities, behavioral testing, inter-agent authentication, memory inspection and automated response workflows.

This sequencing provides a practical starting point—establish visibility and containment first and then deepen prevention and detection.

The strongest contribution of this framework is its operational focus. It asks teams to connect model provenance, agent permissions, runtime activity and incident response rather than assess each in isolation.

Leadership reporting should emphasize measurable coverage and tested effectiveness. Useful measures include the proportion of agents under governance, model integrity verification coverage, supply chain scanning coverage and decommissioning compliance.

These measures should be considered alongside the evidence used to close individual findings, connecting implementation progress to demonstrated control effectiveness.

For enterprise leaders, the goal isn’t to eliminate every uncertainty before deploying AI. It’s to make that uncertainty manageable with accountable ownership, observable actions and tested intervention paths. Governance sets expectations; operational evidence shows whether the organization can enforce them.​

TL;DR: Mortgage rates dropped today, but inflation data could shake things up next week.

With the midterm elections behind us, mortgage rates are continuing their gradual slide this month. One factor is a sell-off in tech stocks, which can send investors toward the relative safety of bonds and help push mortgage rates lower.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 6.96% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is five basis points lower than yesterday and 11 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Meanwhile, a stronger-than-expected jobs report could slow that slide by reinforcing expectations for another Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

And a reminder: While the economy never sleeps, markets are closed on the weekends. The rates you see Friday are unlikely to change much (if at all) until Monday.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

As for what’s next: Tomorrow’s jobs report, showing October data, could potentially nudge mortgage rates in either direction. To understand the link between jobs data and mortgage rates, keep reading below the video.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

The recent slide in mortgage rates might reverse course if next week’s inflation data comes in hot.

This week, the Nerds are watching the October Consumer Price Index, which comes out on Tuesday, Nov. 10. CPI is one of two key measures of inflation, which the Federal Reserve aims to keep in check relative to the strength of the labor market. (The Fed looks more closely at the other data set, the Personal Consumption Expenditures Index, which comes out Nov. 25.)

Right now, the labor market is looking pretty darn healthy: The October jobs report, released today from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, showed U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, far more than economists expected, and unemployment edged down to 4.1%.

Raising the federal funds rate is the Fed’s main tool for bringing inflation down, but rate hikes are only on the table when the labor market is strong enough to handle it. Right now, it’s looking fairly likely that the Fed will approve a rate hike when the committee meets Dec. 8-9. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates directly, but an anticipated rate hike can put upward pressure on mortgage rates, which respond to investors’ expectations for the economy and Fed policy.

Still, a jump in mortgage rates isn’t a sure thing. October’s inflation data will capture the effect of the Fed’s last rate hike, which came in the middle of September. If that worked as expected and inflation shows signs of slowing, mortgage rates will be less affected.

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.46% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#3147. Philips: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Hospitals are consolidating vendors, and Philips is pitching integrated platforms over lowest price, a shift that could define the next contract cycle.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 3, 2026, Philips (PHG -0.52%) announced an 8% increase in equipment order intake. For long-term investors, expanding order books signal that health systems are locking into the company's diagnostic platforms for years to come. Three things management said stand out.

Hospitals are consolidating vendor relationships to streamline operations, giving Philips an advantage in pitching integrated equipment platforms. Management captured market share in North America by replacing long-standing rivals at major hospital networks.

The company is shifting hospital clients away from one-off equipment sales and toward Enterprise Monitoring as a Service (EMaaS), a model in which health systems pay recurring fees for software and hardware. That recurring model helps insulate cash flows from lumpier capital spending cycles.

Rising component costs and wage pressure continue to hit healthcare suppliers, but operational savings are offsetting those headwinds. Management pushed its structural cost-reduction program forward, keeping the business on path to reach its long-term profitability targets.

Equipment orders are expanding across core healthcare markets, supported by helium-free imaging platforms and integrated software. Management relies on strategic customer partnerships to navigate hospital spending while monitoring procurement changes in China.

Disciplined operational execution underpins the multiyear plan for compound annual growth rate, or CAGR, expansion.

#3144. GE Vernova vs. Vistra: Which Industrials Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

GE Vernova boasts a strong balance sheet, while Vistra trades at a lower valuation but carries significant leverage.

GE Vernova (GEV +0.47%) and Vistra (VST +10.55%) both play critical roles in powering the global economy. As energy demand rises, choosing between these two leaders requires a close look at their different business models.

GE Vernova focuses on the technology and equipment required to generate and move electricity worldwide. In contrast, Vistra is a major power producer and retail provider serving millions of customers in the United States. While both benefit from the growing energy needs of data centers, they offer distinct risk and reward profiles for investors.

GE Vernova builds and services the equipment that makes electricity possible, ranging from gas and wind turbines to nuclear reactor technology. The company serves major global utilities and hyperscalers, maintaining an installed base that generates roughly 25% of the world's electricity. It also collaborates with Hitachi (HTHIF +1.54%) on the development of small modular reactors (SMRs) to meet future energy needs through nuclear power.

In its latest annual report covering FY 2025, GE Vernova reported revenue of nearly $38.1 billion, representing growth of roughly 8.9% over the prior year. The company achieved net income of close to $4.9 billion, resulting in an impressive net margin of approximately 12.8%. This performance reflects a steady improvement in profitability as the company scales its electrification and power segments.

Vistra operates as an integrated retail electricity and power generation company, selling both electricity and natural gas to approximately 5 million customers. Its diverse portfolio includes nuclear power, natural gas, and battery storage assets that support large load facilities like oil field operations and data centers. Key retail brands under its umbrella include TXU Energy and Dynegy Energy Services.

For FY 2025, Vistra generated revenue of approximately $17.7 billion, which was a 3% increase compared to the previous fiscal year. Net income for the period reached roughly $944 million, yielding a net margin of close to 5.3%. While these figures are lower than the prior year's results, Vistra remains a significant force among electric utility stocks today.

GE Vernova faces risks related to supply chain disruptions and the volatile costs of critical materials used in its turbines. The company often operates under long-term, fixed-price contracts, which can lead to project losses if labor or material expenses rise unexpectedly. It also faces intense global competition from other equipment manufacturers like Siemens Energy (SMEGF +3.67%) and Mitsubishi Electric (MIELF +2.54%).

Vistra is highly exposed to the price volatility of wholesale power and fuel sources, including natural gas and uranium. The company must also navigate complex regulatory environments regarding carbon emissions and climate change policies. Additionally, its high level of indebtedness requires disciplined financial management to maintain liquidity and meet collateral requirements in competitive energy markets.

Vistra presents a lower entry point based on its earnings multiples, while GE Vernova carries a premium.

Global electricity demand increased by 3% in 2025 compared to 2024, and that trend is only going to continue. And as that demand increases, GE Vernova and Vistra are each positioned to benefit. Both stocks are worth considering as investments, and each could fit together into a portfolio. But if I only had to choose one, I would choose GE Vernova. With increased power demand, GE Vernova serves more of a pick-and-shovel role, selling the infrastructure and components needed for power supply. That leaves it less exposed to regulatory risks compared to if it was directly supplying power.

It is also a quiet player in the nuclear energy space, working on an SMR project with Hitachi. Its BWRX-300 reactor is under construction in Canada, and it's expected to be completed by the end of 2029, with commercial operation before the end of 2030. It's once again positioning itself to be in the right place at the right time, as Precedence Research forecasts that the global nuclear reactor market is expected to grow from $31.5 billion in 2026 to $50.3 billion by 2034.

Also, GE Vernova's market it can serve is larger, as evidenced by its revenue and net income compared to Vistra. Also, its backlog alone, as of the third quarter of 2026, is $197 billion. Adding all that up- from its pick-and-shovel nature, which can avoid certain risks, to being at the forefront of building SMRs, to its backlog- I would rather own GE Vernova.
