#3142. 19 Startup Habits Tech Companies Should Never Outgrow

Startups often move quickly because they have to, making the most of limited resources and adapting as circumstances change. As tech companies scale, added layers of process, approval and hierarchy can gradually slow decision making and erode the flexibility that helped them grow.

The good news is that companies don’t have to abandon the habits that fueled their early success as they expand. Here, Forbes Technology Council members share startup habits established tech companies should preserve—or relearn—to maintain their agility as they grow.

Established tech companies should preserve the startup habit of staying close to the raw customer experience. As organizations scale, dashboards and layers of interpretation can obscure what people actually struggle with. Leaders should keep speaking directly with customers and empower small teams to act quickly on what they learn. Scale should improve execution, not distance companies from users. - Leah Wang, Karpo

The tech market in the AI era is changing super fast—the cycles for product demands, work methods and tools, and customers’ needs and requirements have all become very short. The one thing companies must preserve is agility within the boundaries of their focus. It is easy to get lost and try to achieve everything, only to end up with nothing. Being able to stay agile while knowing the problem your company solves is critical. - Yoav Amitai, Elsight

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Startups are great at prototyping new products and services and moving on quickly from ideas during the research and development phase. As companies scale, this “create fast, test fast, decide fast” capacity is often diminished. One way to keep it alive is to engage early with a customer or partner to confirm requirements or do testing. It puts healthy pressure on the development process while gathering valuable external feedback on pricing, functionality and positioning. - Eva Rudin, Thales Cybersecurity

Preserve the willingness to challenge assumptions. Startups move quickly because they don’t treat “this is how it’s done” as an acceptable answer. As companies scale, process can quietly replace curiosity. The best teams keep questioning their own products, decisions and assumptions, especially when something appears to be working. Scale should give you more resources to challenge the status quo, not more reasons to protect it. - Alissa Knight, Assail, Inc.

Keep saying no to the wrong business. When you are small, you cannot serve everyone, so you get good at turning down the wrong customers and use cases, and that focus is half of why you survive. At scale, every deal looks worth taking, and the muscle for walking away weakens. You must protect it on purpose. The companies that keep rejecting what does not fit stay sharp long after they could afford to lose focus. - Vytautas Savickas, Oxylabs

Solve problems close to where they occur. As organizations scale, issues often get escalated to the most senior person rather than the person best connected to the customer or the detail of the issue. That introduces delays to fixes being made and promotes permission-seeking rather than judgment and accountability. Push authority down and let the people closest to the problem make the call. - Rob Sloan, Zscaler

Knowing when to stop is crucial. Startups have to focus because their resources are limited. The ability in a startup to know exactly what is going on means not only decisions to invest but also decisions to divest are made faster. - Véronique Özkaya, DATAmundi

AI-first thinking is the biggest thing established players need to adopt from the startup realm. New ventures have the luxury of AI being the starting point, not something they need to bolt onto old, outdated processes. That blank slate is a real edge—no legacy systems standing between them and AI-driven gains. So, I’d begin every problem by asking where AI can make the biggest impact and build from there. That mindset will define the future enterprise. - Tarek Nseir, Valliance

Preserve the habit of testing before debating. Startups rarely have enough data to eliminate uncertainty, so they build something small, put it in front of users, and learn. At scale, debate can become a substitute for discovery. Established companies should relearn how to turn unanswered questions into fast, low-risk experiments, using evidence from the market to resolve what meetings cannot. - Melissa King, Paylocity

Let the people closest to a problem try things without asking permission first. In many cases, our team members have made our most impactful suggestions. We discussed it, tried it out and looked at the results together. Nobody wrote a proposal. Give teams a sandbox, clear data and security rules, and a few weeks to test. You’ll learn more than you would from a six-month planning cycle. - Merav Yuravlivker, Data Society

Keep communication lines efficient. The best startups have an uncanny ability to throw unnecessary hierarchy to the wind and flatten communication lines. That’s how startups home in on solutions rather than simply admiring the problem. - James Stanger, CompTIA

Cross-department talk is essential. In a startup, everyone can talk to everyone without wondering about politics and the org chart. You never know where the next good idea will come from—it often comes from an “unexpected part” of the org chart. If Joe from team X is afraid of talking to Mary from team Y just because they don’t have the same boss, the company’s capacity to innovate is severely impacted. - Stephane Donze, AODocs

Startups move fast because they accept higher risk, while large organizations slow down to protect reputation, revenue and investors. As companies grow, they must consciously balance risk appetite to keep innovating. Teams should also keep the startup habit of “relentless iteration”—sharing early “sh***y first drafts,” as referenced by Brené Brown—for fast feedback instead of waiting for polish. - Mandy Andress, Elastic

Ship things that aren’t ready and learn from real users instead of extensive internal reviews. Process exists to prevent mistakes, but it also prevents speed and discovery. Talk directly to users without a layer of research, summaries or account managers in between. - Amy Gu, Dynamsoft

Create rituals early and maintain them throughout your growth. Startup life is hard. One of the things that inspires and preserves team alignment is the rituals created in early startup life that create an identity, a battle cry and a touchstone to the mission. As new employees join the company, these same rituals become part of their orientation, which helps encourage unity. - Amy Brown, Authenticx

Preserve fast, reversible decision making. Let teams run small, bounded tests without routing every choice through layers of approval, then use the results to adjust quickly. Reserve heavyweight reviews for decisions that are costly or difficult to undo—not every experiment. - Nagesh Nama, xLM Continuous Intelligence

Share the full picture with everyone. In a startup, the whole team knows the revenue, the biggest customer problem, and what worries the founders most. As companies grow, that context gets held back at the top, and teams start working on tasks without knowing why they matter. People make better decisions when they know what the company is facing. - Asad Khan, TestMu AI

Preserve the startup habit of a hard work-in-progress limit. Early teams cannot pursue 20 “top priorities,” so starting one thing means stopping another. At scale, portfolios expand faster than capacity, and coordination becomes the bottleneck. Force every new priority to displace an old one. Speed comes as much from limiting concurrency as from moving faster. - Akhilesh Sharma, A3Logics Inc.

Do it by hand before automating it. Startups run a new process manually for a few weeks and learn where it actually breaks. Larger companies jump straight to automation and lock in their guesses. In mature organizations we audit, roughly a third of flows either duplicate another or barely run. A month of manual work first is cheaper than a year of maintaining the wrong automation. - Sergii Grushai, Peeklogic

#3129. The S&P 500 Just Fell More Than 4% in a Day From Near Its Record. Here's What Happened Next in 2 Similar Situations Since 1950.

The only two close matches are 1955 and 1989. A year later, they were nothing alike.

The S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.31%) fell 4.36% on Thursday, Nov. 5, ending at 7,353.73. It was the index's worst day since April 4, 2025, when it lost nearly 6%.

What made Thursday's drop unusual was where it started. The index had closed Wednesday at 7,688.62, under 2% off its record close of 7,818.93 on Oct. 6.

Tech shares led the way down, and chip stocks fell hardest, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index losing around 12%.

Two poor chipmaker reports and a midterm election that had investors nervous about new limits on artificial intelligence data centers both hurt the group.

I wanted to check how rare this mix is. Looking through Yahoo Finance's daily closing prices (dividends left out), I counted 56 earlier days since 1950 when the S&P 500 dropped 4% or more. Only two of them began with the index within 2% of a record close. One was Sept. 26, 1955, and the other was Oct. 13, 1989.

The 1955 drop was on the first trading day after word of President Dwight Eisenhower's heart attack. The S&P 500 had closed at a record the Friday before, and it fell around 6.6% that Monday.

The year that followed went pretty smoothly. A month later, the index was flat. It was up around 6% after three months and about 13% after six.

And a year after the drop (252 trading days), it was up about 7%. Even its lowest close in that time was only about 4% below where it ended on Sept. 26.

The 1989 drop came on a Friday the 13th. That day, the group behind a $6.75 billion labor-management buyout of UAL, the parent of United Airlines, couldn't get enough financing. The S&P 500 fell around 6.1% that day, from about 1.2% below the record close it set on Oct. 9.

The year that followed was rockier. The index was up around 2% a month later and about 3% after six months. But it was down about 10% a year after the drop, as the economy slipped into the 1990-1991 recession. At its lowest close over that year, the index was around 11% below its Oct. 13 level.

In short, the two closest matches split. Two cases can't say much by themselves.

The broader record looks a lot better. Of the 56 earlier drops of 4% or more since 1950, 47 were followed by a higher index 12 months on, with a median gain of around 23%. And the odds improved the longer investors waited. The index was up a month later in 36 of the 56 cases, after three months in 41, after six months in 43, and after a year in 47.

Of course, most of these drops came in very different conditions. In 47 of the 56 cases, the index was already at least 10% below its record when the drop hit, and the typical one started around 24% below it. Over a third of them (21) came during 2008 and 2009 alone.

This 23% median gain, then, mainly reflects rebounds from deep in sell-offs that were already well underway. Thursday's drop started from near the peak.

Limit the list to drops that began within 5% of a record, and five cases are left (1955, 1986, 1989, 1997, and 2018). Four of the five were up a year later. But the median gain was around 7%, well below the full group's.

Sure, five cases is still a tiny sample. But I think it's a fair reminder that the largest rebounds in this record followed much bigger falls than the one investors just saw.

Even after Thursday, the S&P 500 is up around 7% in 2026 as I write, and it's about 6% off its Oct. 6 record. Its price-to-earnings ratio, at around 25, is also far above its long-term median of about 15.

In the end, this history doesn't point in one direction. And the wider record arguably looks strong partly because most of its big drops started from much lower levels.

I wouldn't sell an S&P 500 index fund over Thursday's drop. For a buy-and-hold investor, selling after a 4% day has usually meant missing what came next, as 47 of the 56 earlier cases were up a year later.

But I also wouldn't count on a 20%-plus rise from here just because so many past drops were followed by one. Starting this close to a record, and at that valuation, the lower gain after 1955 or even the loss after 1989 might be the more realistic guide.

#3124. Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling

A version of the S&P 500 without AI briefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market.

A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking the S&P 500 without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading.

Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500. That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up.

Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle. Shares of Meta Platforms sank almost 7% Thursday after it outlined more plans to spend heavily on capex and issue additional shares.

Companies supplying power and equipment for the buildout have been hit hard — names like GE Vernova, Bloom Energy, Vistra and Quanta Services all suffered steep declines during the recent selloff.

Goldman, which launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, uses the S&P 500 as its starting universe and excludes companies perceived to be enablers of AI before applying S&P 500 Index weighting methodology to the remaining universe of companies.

The ex-AI index lagged the S&P 500 for most of the year as investors continued to favor chipmakers, cloud-computing companies and other firms benefiting from heavy AI spending. However, that advantage has been narrowing and it disappeared last week.

Meanwhile, investors are rotating into defensive areas. ETFs like State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF, State Street Health Select SPDR ETF and State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF are up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is ahead 10% too, though that's more related to the war in Iran.

Some analysts recommend sticking with non-AI companies for diversification and protection against more pain in tech. The "AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure over the last two weeks," Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in a note on Oct. 24.

Two industries that Oppenheimer favors now are commercial services and insurance. The firm upgraded those industries to overweight last week, recommending Republic Services, Cintas, Verisk Analytics, Broadridge Financial Solutions, MetLife and Arthur J. Gallagher.

Berkshire Hathaway is also capitalizing on the rotation out of tech. Its Class B shares are up 8% this month, though it's still lagging behind the S&P 500 this year.

Berkshire owns a wide swath of operating companies, including insurance giant Geico and Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad. It also has a $364 billion stock portfolio including companies like Apple, Coca-Cola, Alphabet and Bank of America. That diversification may help Berkshire continue to outperform if the tech sector drags down the S&P 500.

Trivector Research sees potential in "non-tech compounders." Healthcare giant Eli Lilly is one idea. The stock is up 22% on the strength of Lilly's weight-loss drugs. The company has more in the pipeline, including a next-generation obesity drug that Lilly plans to file for FDA approval early in 2027.

Viking Holdings, a cruise operator, is also proving durable. The company said on its August earnings call that 40% of its river capacity and 60% of its ocean capacity was already booked for 2027. "Based on recent events, we've seen our guests have proved to be resilient and are continuing to book 2027 and future seasons," the company told investors.

Viking stock is up 15% this year but it may still have upside. The average Wall Street target is $109, above recent prices around $82. Barclays recently upgraded the cruise operator to overweight with a $102 target, citing the company's "compelling risk/reward."

#3118. Think Arm Is Too Expensive? 1 Thing You Need To Understand About the Chip Stock

Investors still don't seem to appreciate Arm's upside potential.

Like the rest of the semiconductor sector, Arm Holdings (ARM +4.74%) endured a brutal sell-off on Thursday.

Shares of the chip stock, which is best known for licensing its power-efficient CPU architecture, lost 13% on Thursday following its fiscal second-quarter earnings report.

That sell-off was largely driven by the broader plunge in tech stocks on concerns about potential data center restrictions following the midterm elections, though Arm shares fell in after-hours trading on Wednesday after the report came out.

Arm topped estimates on the top and bottom lines, but investors were disappointed with weak growth in royalty revenue, which rose 8% to $670 million, a function of a slow smartphone market. Arm dominates the smartphone CPU market with virtually 100% market share, and it’s still the biggest source of royalty revenue for the company. However, higher memory prices have pressured smartphone shipments, and smartphone royalty revenue was roughly flat in the year.

Nonetheless, the company’s growth markets continued to deliver strong results. Data center royalty revenue doubled year-over-year, and now makes up roughly a quarter of total royalty revenue. Physical AI royalty revenue, meanwhile, was up 50%, driven by growth in the auto market.

Guidance for royalty revenue growth in the third quarter was also disappointing, as the company forecast just low-single-digit royalty growth due to weakness in the smartphone segment and tough comparisons with the quarter a year ago.

License revenue in the quarter was strong, up 50% to $773 million, driven by an increase in long-term agreements. Arm’s total revenue rose 27% to $1.44 billion, topping the consensus at $1.38 billion. On the bottom line, adjusted earnings per share rose from $0.39 to $0.52, which beat estimates at $0.48.

Arm stock soared in March when the company announced that it was getting into silicon for the first time. Historically, the company has just licensed its CPU architecture and collected revenue on royalties. Now, it will design its own chips like fabless peers such as Nvidia, AMD, and Broadcom.

Arm introduced the Arm AGI CPU with Meta Platforms as its lead partner. The data center CPU has a higher performance per watt than any current competitors on the market, and will go into production in Arm’s fiscal fourth quarter, which ends next March. The company already has more demand than it can handle and raised its revenue guidance from the chip through fiscal 2028 from $1 billion to $2 billion. By fiscal 2031, it expects $15 billion in annual revenue from Arm AGI CPU.

The company said in its shareholder letter that it’s more confident in hitting that $2 billion forecast, and it’s focused on “expanding capacity to meet growing customer demand.”

CPU demand is directly correlated with AI inference, which is what powers agentic AI. There’s a lot of upside potential for the new AGI CPU if a product like Meta’s Muse gains significant adoption.

Arm CFO Jason Child explained that every Muse user required a single CPU core devoted to it. If Meta were able to convert every one of its roughly 3.5 billion social media users into Meta users, it would need to buy 3.5 billion Arm AGI CPU cores from Arm. Child said that cores are priced between $10 and $20, which would translate into $35 billion-$70 billion in revenue.

That’s the ceiling from Muse, and not every Facebook user is going to adopt Muse, of course, but the example is illustrative of Arm’s potential growth with the new CPU. It also shows that the addressable CPU market is potentially much larger than the $100 billion or $200 billion previously estimated, as there are several personal AI agents on the market and agentic AI products will certainly expand.

Arm stock has fallen sharply since it peaked in June, following a broad rally in chip stocks and excitement about CPU demand. It’s still expensive, with a price-to-earnings ratio of around 80, but the discussion of the stock seems to ignore the upside potential related to the Arm AGI CPU.

While investors will still have to wait a couple of quarters to get some meaningful numbers on the AGI CPU, it could bring in much more than $15 billion in revenue by fiscal 2031. At this point, owning Arm for some exposure to the agentic AI upside makes sense, even if the stock otherwise looks expensive.

#3117. Giannis Antetokounmpo is ‘difficult’ to coach: Doc Rivers

Retired NBA coach Doc Rivers is never afraid to speak the truth, and Giannis Antetokounmpo is on his mind these days.

Rivers explained on the "Bill Simmons Podcast" that Antetokounmpo is a "difficult guy" after having coached him for a season and a half before retiring in April 2026.

"He's not easy," Rivers said of coaching Antetokounmpo. "He plays at this crazy downhill pace. He's really a difficult guy. He has this great passing ability, but he doesn't have super IQ at the same time. He really has one way. Every play, he wants to force it."

Giannis Antetokounmpo of the Miami Heat shoots a free throw during a game against the Golden State Warriors in San Francisco on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

Antetokounmpo is an ultra-rare physical specimen, earning the nickname "The Greek Freak," standing 6-foot-11 and weighing 250 pounds.

His time in Milwaukee is mostly considered a success, as he won an NBA title in 2021, but the end of his career with Rivers was frustrating. The Bucks had nearly no assets to acquire new players and Antetokounmpo himself was a constant source of trade conjecture.

"I wished he learned how to execute better," Rivers said. "The thing he needs to still learn is the value of execution. How important it is when you're in practice and shoot around to lock in on execution. Now he has a coach who's as good as there is in execution."

The Bucks finally did trade him to the Miami Heat this past offseason and he's hooked up with coach Erik Spoelstra, though early returns have not been good with a 3-6 record.

"For the team to work, you have to learn how to execute," Rivers said.

Rivers has always been honest when talking about players he's coaching, including when he's still with the team.

Head coach Doc Rivers and Giannis Antetokounmpo #34 of the Milwaukee Bucks look on against the Brooklyn Nets during the game at Barclays Center on December 08, 2024 in New York Getty Images

As the 76ers coach, Rivers had a blunt answer to a reporter after Ben Simmons passed up a wide-open layup in Game 7 of a playoff game against the Atlanta Hawks in 2021.

The reporter asked whether Rivers still believed in Simmons to be an elite point guard on a championship-winning team.

"I don't know that question or the answer to that right now," Rivers replied after they lost to a clearly inferior Hawks team that went on to not be a contender in the years following. "So I don't know the answer to that."

Simmons refused to show up the following year and was eventually traded to the Nets for James Harden before falling out of the league in a detrimental chain of events for his career.

Simmons later said Rivers' comments infuriated him.

Doc Rivers has never been one to clam up when talking about his players. USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con

"How did I feel? I was like, 'What a piece of s—t," Simmons said of Rivers' blunt comments in a recent documentary "Ben Being Ben". "When times get tough, people start panicking. People throw people under the bus, and that's just what happened."

Antetokounmpo and the Heat face the floundering Kings on Sunday after losing to the Warriors on Thursday.

#3114. Hims & Hers Health vs. Intuitive Surgical: Which Healthcare Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Both are disruptors, but one of these growth stocks stands out over the other.

Investors seeking long-term growth often weigh the disruptive potential of telehealth against the proven dominance of medical robotics. Choosing between Hims & Hers Health (HIMS +8.06%) and Intuitive Surgical (ISRG -3.35%) depends on your appetite for risk and valuation.

Both companies operate within the healthcare sector but serve different ends of the market. Hims & Hers Health focuses on direct-to-consumer digital wellness and personalized prescriptions. Intuitive Surgical builds the complex hardware and software systems that surgeons use to perform minimally invasive procedures in hospitals around the world.

Hims & Hers Health operates a digital platform that connects patients with licensed healthcare providers. The company sells personalized treatment plans for hair loss, sexual health, mental health, and weight loss. Its business model relies on a substantial majority of revenue from recurring subscription purchases of prescription medications. By utilizing partner pharmacies for fulfillment and affiliated medical groups for consultations, the company maintains a scalable infrastructure.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $2.3 billion, representing a growth rate of approximately 59% compared to the previous year. This rapid expansion followed a strong FY 2024, where revenue reached close to $1.5 billion. The company reported net income of roughly $128.4 million for the 2025 fiscal period. This performance marks a significant shift toward profitability after reporting a net loss in earlier years.

Intuitive Surgical is a leader among medical device stocks due to its da Vinci surgical system. This platform allows for robotic-assisted surgery, which often leads to shorter recovery times for patients. The company generates revenue through system sales, recurring service contracts, and the sale of disposable instruments. Its primary customers are large hospitals and health systems that integrate these platforms into their operating rooms.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $10 billion, which is a 20.5% increase over the prior year. The company reported a net income of approximately $2.9 billion, resulting in a net margin of roughly 28.4%. This high net margin reflects the percentage of revenue that remains as profit after all expenses are paid. The steady growth in procedure volumes continues to drive the demand for new systems and ongoing instrument replacement.

Hims & Hers Health faces significant regulatory and legal scrutiny, particularly regarding its compounded weight-loss products. Investigations by the DOJ and potential FDA restrictions could disrupt its core operations. The company also depends heavily on third-party medical groups and pharmacies for fulfillment. Furthermore, it is currently involved in patent infringement litigation with Novo Nordisk and competes against well-funded incumbents in a market where brand differentiation is difficult to maintain.

Intuitive Surgical faces competition from major players such as Medtronic (MDT -2.90%) and Johnson & Johnson. These rivals are developing their own robotic surgical platforms, which could lead to pricing pressure. The company is also managing ongoing product liability and antitrust litigation, including a recent $450 million settlement charge. Because its revenue model depends on procedure volumes, any global disruption to elective surgeries or hospital budget cuts poses a risk to its financial results.

While Hims & Hers Health appears more affordable based on its sales multiple, Intuitive Surgical trades at a significantly lower multiple of its future earnings estimates.

With both of these companies in the medical field, they carry noticeable risk, so it is best to treat each as a more speculative position. For instance, neither company is performing particularly well in 2026, with the share price of Intuitive down 17.2%, while the share price of Hims & Hers is down nearly 26%. But if there could only be one winner between the two, I would lean toward picking Intuitive. The main reason is the uniqueness of its product offerings and the moat that it has created. Being a trusted equipment provider in robot-assisted surgery, even if there is some growing competition, helps create a moat, as not just anyone can build a similar company and instantly receive orders from hospitals. And being that trusted provider helps lead to more repeat customers. For instance, in the third quarter of 2026, Intuitive grew its da Vinci surgical system installed base to 12,094 systems, an increase of 12% compared to the prior-year period. Intuitive also reported revenue of $3 billion for the quarter, an increase of 22%.

In comparison, Hims & Hers has a narrower moat, serving more as a platform that connects consumers with products. It's also becoming an increasingly competitive space, with pharmaceutical companies launching their own direct-to-consumer and direct-to-patient platforms, such as Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk. To reemphasize, both of these companies have their challenges and should be considered more speculative positions. But Intuitive stands out for its better moat.

The Golden State Warriors Kristaps Porzingis saga is expected to come to an end before the end of the year, according to a report by Brett Siegel of ClutchPoints. Porzingis, who re-signed with the Dubs last season on a partially guaranteed two-year, $40 million deal, opted not to join the team for training camp and has accepted not receiving payments, seemingly deciding to retire. Siegel notes that players who signed free agent contracts this offseason will all become trade-eligible on December 15th, which will also give teams more options on that day. Moreover, December 16th is the deadline for a player to be traded and still be eligible to be aggregated in a deal at the trade deadline in February. So while it's definitely possible for a deal to be made sooner, that effectively becomes the deadline for the Warriors front office if they would like to make a smaller move with Porzingis that would leave them flexibility to still go looking for bigger fish at the deadline.

Siegel's reporting does not even engage with a scenario where the Warriors do not trade Porzingis in December. #3112. Sweetgreen Is Finally Growing Again. Time To Buy?

Sweetgreen posted same-store sales growth in October. Is it the beginning of a turnaround?

After nearly two years of declining same-store sales, Sweetgreen (SG +3.98%) has returned to growth.

While the company's third-quarter performance was marred by the Cyclospora outbreak, management said that October results were positive, with same-store sales up 5% and traffic up 4%. Is this a buy signal for the fast-casual stock? Let's take a look at the third-quarter results and discuss the company's prospects moving forward.

Sweetgreen's third quarter was reminiscent of the brand's recent struggles, though most of the numbers can be pinned on the Cyclospora outbreak, which did not directly affect Sweetgreen but dissuaded consumers from visiting salad chains. Sweetgreen was implicated by association.

Same-store sales in the quarter fell 6.4%, and revenue ticked up 2.1% to $176 million, which beat estimates at $169.4 million. Restaurant-level profit margin fell from 13.1% to 10.4%, and its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) loss expanded from $4.4 million to $6.8 million.

On a generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) basis, its per-share loss narrowed from $0.31 to $0.26, which was slightly better than expectations of a loss of $0.27 per share. CEO Jonathan Neman redirected investor focus to the future, saying, "We believe our Sweet Growth Transformation Plan is beginning to take hold, with sales improving through the quarter and positive comparable sales in October, primarily driven by transaction growth."

Sweetgreen raised its guidance for the full year, calling for same-store sales to be down 5.5%, better than a previous range of -7% to-8%, implying 3.4% growth in the fourth quarter. It sees 10 net new restaurant openings and an adjusted EBITDA loss of $20 million-$23 million, compared to an earlier range of a $23 million-$27 million loss.

Now that Sweetgreen has returned to same-store sales growth, the next goal is to return to margin growth, assuming it can maintain the comparable sales growth.

The company is still significantly underwater from its peak in 2024. Its average unit volume (sales per restaurant) clocked in at $2.47 million in the third quarter, down from $2.92 million at the end of 2024. To get back there, Sweetgreen will have to grow same-store sales by nearly 20%, which could take several years, and open new stores with solid AUVs. Sweetgreen reported a restaurant-level profit margin of 17% in 2024 and expected it to rise to 20% in 2025, before it ran into a raft of challenges, causing the stock to plummet.

Following the successful launch of its wraps this spring, Sweetgreen is relaunching its plates menu, which includes dishes like rotisserie chicken and caramelized garlic steak, as part of a strategy to grow its dinner business and diversify further away from salads. Management also said it expected restaurant-level profit margins to benefit from more efficient labor and supply chain spending.

Sweetgreen stock rose 4% on Friday as investors applauded the improved guidance and return to growth. The stock currently trades at a price-to-sales ratio of 2, meaning if it achieved a 10% profit margin, it would have a price-to-earnings ratio of 20.

Sweetgreen is a long way from achieving such a profit margin, but the company still has a lot of growth potential. While the company has slowed its new store openings to work on operations, it still sees room in the market for at least 1,000 locations, more than triple the 290 it currently has.

If it can move toward that goal while growing same-store sales and improving profitability, the stock should be a long-term winner.

Jeremy Bowman has positions in Sweetgreen. The Motley Fool recommends Sweetgreen. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3109. Lyntris (LYNX) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Backlog doubled this year as international demand reshaped the growth outlook.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Lyntris Inc. (LYNX +28.66%) reported third quarter results characterized by significant revenue growth and a more than twofold increase in total backlog since the start of the fiscal year. Management reported that expansion is occurring across all mission domains, particularly within the Air & Missile Defense and Space ISR & Resilient Communications segments, which both saw triple-digit revenue growth. The company stated that its merchant supplier model allows it to support multiple prime contractors while maintaining high ownership of design intellectual property, which accounts for 85% of product revenue. Following its August IPO, the company has reduced its net leverage ratio to 1.2x and established a new $300 million credit facility to support future working capital needs and strategic initiatives.

Matthew Alty: Thank you, Tim. Let's now turn to Slide 7. I'd like to start by taking a step back and examining the mission environment because it explains why customers choose Lyntris. I was just curious to get your guys' thoughts on the capital allocation strategy going forward, just given that free cash flow was strong during the quarter and year-to-date, but there's debt on the balance sheet, but leverage is in a healthy position. So how are you guys thinking about that?

Brian Morrison: Yes. So I agree with you that I am comfortable with our leverage position where it is. And I'll note, of course, that we're growing and naturally delevering. Now as to capital allocation, you're right to note that there's cash on the balance sheet. And the way Matt and I think about capital allocation is roughly as follows: One, we have a disciplined strategic view of technologies that we're interested in and technology areas where we want to be. So we will deploy capital to access those technology nodes either through M&A or through IRAD. Now that said, those are, I think, the principal ways in which we would deploy capital.

I think it's also possible that we would do some opportunistic share repurchase, where we think that we are undervalued in the market. If we have cash, we might do some share repurchase in the future after running the appropriate regulatory traps for that. I don't think that there is a possibility that we would use that excess cash to delever because we're already delevering from growth and I don't anticipate that we would use that cash for a dividend. But aside from those exceptions, I think we're just always looking for the highest and best use of our precious cash and our shareholder capital. Matt, do you want to add anything to that?

Matthew Alty: I think you covered it, right.

Andrew Steinhardt: Got you. That's very helpful. And I guess -- just a quick follow-up. Can you talk about the Minnesota Tech hub? What sort of products will actually be developed there and why St. Paul?

Brian Morrison: Yes. So we recognized that location as a great source of talent, particularly in some emerging work we're doing in both health care and in radars. The health care part of the business is a small part of the business, but it's important. It's about cutting-edge solutions for military health care going forward. We're also looking to put some of our radar work into that location. It's just a great source of talent, and we've had really good relationships with the Minnesota community, and that's sort of what led us there.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our next question comes from the line of Peter Arment with Baird.

Peter Arment: Nice results. Brian, the -- both the Air & Missile Defense, and Space revenues were kind of materially above, I think, kind of Street expectations. Any specific programs that you can highlight that are really driving that? I mean, LTAMDS, obviously, I know is ramping. Is that one of the key programs? Or any color there would be really helpful.

Brian Morrison: Yes. It is not limited to any one program, Peter. You're right. It's pretty broad across the mission area. That said, you're right. LTAMDS is growing. We have an Air & Missile Defense radar program that is in initial fielding that is growing in significant ways. And in space, our space payload business is going kind of gangbusters, and that's driving accelerated growth there.

Peter Arment: And then just as a quick follow-up, back to kind of the margin question. So it sounds like mix is the big driver here, just a lot more volume on the top line, but some of the design development work is kind of carry. So the 15.4% at the midpoint for margins for this year for adjusted EBITDA. So is that the kind of new jumping off point? Or does this mix begin to evolve back to what you expected?

Brian Morrison: So I think the mix will evolve back to what we've expected over time. I don't want to get into providing '27 guidance at this moment. And I think any precision on that would be a little bit premature. That said, we are only taking work that has real strategic enduring value. And if it helps us on the top line and the EBITDA dollars, but has somewhat compression effect on the margin in the short term, I think that's a trade we will make when it has strategic value. Matt, do you want to add anything?

Matthew Alty: Yes. The only thing that I would add, just thinking ahead over the next few quarters, a lot of the IP that we are developing are really cornerstone elements then of those future systems. So we're confident as we complete the development of this kind of core IP, we'll see margin benefit from it as we see kind of follow-on work on those same kind of opportunities.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Michael Ciarmoli with Guggenheim.

Michael Ciarmoli: Congrats on nice results out of the gate here. Maybe just -- we've commonly heard from investors about maybe some top line growth hesitation. You put out a pretty kind of sporty expectation for a multiyear revenue CAGR. Just in light of kind of what we've seen out of the gate, the guidance, it certainly sounds like you're not going to be short on any growth opportunities, kind of what you just said, developing more cornerstone IP. Do we think about this kind of revenue CAGR kind of accelerating? Or just maybe help us because it seems like the growth here and the guidance is materially higher than expectations.

So just trying to get a sense of how this growth environment evolves here over the coming periods.

Brian Morrison: Yes, I appreciate the question. So we'll be back in early '27 to provide '27 guidance. But what I can tell you now is Matt, Tim and I are completely comfortable with the idea that we will grow 30% or more '26 to '27, which is I think what kind of underlies your question. Fair question, given that we blew it out of the water here in Q3, and we've got good guidance for full year, but I still feel confident in that 30%.

Michael Ciarmoli: And then maybe just back to the margin question. You kind of used that term that the space payloads are going gangbusters. And I tend to think of those larger, more sophisticated payloads carrying a little bit more risk. Is it fair to say that you've got some more conservative booking rates on those programs? Is that also a factor in the margin? As you get maybe closer to delivery or execute on milestones, we could see some management reserve release there?

Matthew Alty: Yes. I don't want to get into the specifics of management reserve. But what I would say is just back to my earlier comment, when you think about those space payloads or kind of any of the key programs that we're supporting, there are key elements of the IP that we will invest into early that we are very, very confident then are applicable to future opportunities. A great example would be one of our recent acquisitions where we acquired a business that brought us motion control technology for some of the antenna that we would use in our space applications.

The investment into that technology will be directly applicable to a whole range of resilient solutions that we'll field either in space or on ground applications. So for sure, as we take that IP, invest into it now and then apply it to future wins, we're very, very confident we'll see margin growth as we do that.

Brian Morrison: Yes. I think Matt's right. I think we think of that space payload business, that space payload part of the business as a franchise. And as we are developing and designing, testing technologies for today's customer, they will be applicable to the payload pipeline that we have that is robust that will develop -- that will result in better margins going forward on that future work. That is not to say that we're not always looking at our management reserves and our EACs on any given project as it goes forward to get margin growth, but that just gives you a sense of how we think about it.

Matthew Alty: Yes. I would just kind of add to Brian's point there. I would think of this more in terms of nonrecurring engineering NREs that we are thinking through as we kind of bid that work. And we just kind of look at that and say, "Hey, we'll invest into this NRE", knowing that it's going to allow us to win work in the future and not reoccur that NRE, which then drives improved margin on those future orders.

Operator: Our last question comes from the line of Amit Daryanani with Evercore.

Amit Daryanani: Perfect. I guess I'll ask an EBITDA margin question as well. I ask -- on EBITDA margin, if I look at September quarter at 14.7%, can you talk about how much of a headwind [Technical Difficulty] the engineering cost you're talking about 100 basis points of margin expansion is a bit of a stretch goal. But could you spend some time on talking about levers that actually enable EBITDA margin expansion to get back to the TWO handle overtime? I think it would be helpful to just understand what you think the EBITDA margin expansion from here. And my second one on...

Brian Morrison: Can I just pause for a second. Operator, I did not hear most of that. It came through garbled. Did it come through garbled for you?

Operator: Yes. I was wondering if there is a possible solution for the line of the analyst. Let's see.

Brian Morrison: Can you describe that a little better?

Amit Daryanani: Yes. I think, Brian, you just talk about EBITDA margins in September at 14.7%. How much were the engineering R&D headwinds that you folks had? Can you just talk about that? And then conceptually to get EBITDA margins to a two handle over time, what are the building blocks [Technical Difficulty] to what are the different set of things to kind of get to the higher margins over time? And then my follow-up just to understand the backlog. Was there any shift in duration that drove the uptick in backlog, that would be helpful as well.

Brian Morrison: Yes. I'll start with the last question, which is, was there any shift in duration on the backlog? There was not a meaningful change in what we think of as our weighted average period of performance. So I think backlog comparisons here are fair. There's no sort of 7-year award that has dropped into the backlog and affected it in a meaningful way. So then I think the first part of your question was what are the real levers to driving margin rates higher?

And I think they're as follows: One, we have talked, I think, somewhat less on this call than I might have anticipated about our really rapidly growing international business, which is somewhat more accretive from a margin perspective. It's also true that we're signing ever more firm fixed price work, which although it carries some modest amount of increased risk, it also carries the reward of higher margin rates. As our revenue is growing at this high rate, of course, we see operational leverage as we move forward, and we'll look for that to drive our margin rates going forward.

And then finally, we are really at an inflection point, and you see it first in our space business, but there's other places where I think we'll soon be seeing it, where we're really recognizing the power and capability of the entire company on a job-over-job basis. And what that means is that we're able to do more and more for the customer, and that work generates a higher margin because it's higher value for the customer. Matt, do you want to add anything to that?

Matthew Alty: I would just build upon that last comment you made. I mean, our space payload is a great example of that, where we've moved from individual antenna solutions to now integrated antennas that kind of are built for a very, very specific mission requirement. And now we're taking that and building that into an integrated payload. That obviously comes with both revenue and margin benefit as we move up that value chain to a higher-level assembly.

Operator: Thank you. This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

#3107. Better Stock Split to Buy: Meta Platforms vs. Sandisk

Sandisk and Meta's stock splits are being done in two different manners.

Meta Platforms (META +0.84%) and Sandisk (SNDK +3.55%) are each going through a stock split over the next few months. Sandisk is going through a traditional stock split, splitting its shares eight-for-one, effective Nov. 19. Meta's is a bit different. Instead of doing a traditional stock split of its existing stock, it's creating a new share class. This complicates things, but it's still going through a split at the end of the day.

So, which one makes the most sense to invest in? Let's take a look.

First, let's look at what's going on with Meta's stock. Its stock split is a bit goofy, but makes sense in the end. Overall, it's splitting its stock essentially two-for-one. It's doing this by creating a new Class C share. Class C shares will have the same value as Class A shares (the same ones any investor can buy on the market) initially, but in practice they will be worth slightly less over the long term.

The difference between Class C and Class A shares is that the new Class C shares have no voting power. This is important for Meta because, as it hands out Class C shares for acquisitions or employee compensation, CEO Mark Zuckerberg doesn't lose his voting control. This could be a red flag for some investors, but it's the direction that Meta is heading.

If you look at other stocks with split-share structures, like Alphabet (GOOG +0.78%) (GOOGL +0.78%), one share class trades at a discount to the other, but it's not a big enough price difference to be a big deal. So, if you're fine with the voting power of the company residing in the founder's hands, then this is nothing more than your run-of-the-mill two-for-one stock split. But if you're concerned about where Mark Zuckerberg is taking Meta, then it may be time to abandon ship.

For the remainder of the analysis, I'll assume that the average investor is OK with Zuckerberg's controlling power. But even with that, is it enough to be a better stock to own than Sandisk?

Sandisk and Meta aren't even close to being in the same industry. The closest relationship is Meta being a customer of Sandisk's, as it would buy solid-state drives (SSDs) from Sandisk for its data centers. Sandisk makes these devices, which have been in short supply due to the intensity of the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out. This has caused prices on these units to soar, and Sandisk has experienced huge growth as a result. During its latest quarter, revenue soared 378% year over year. That's simply incredible, and trumps anything Meta has delivered.

During Meta's Q3, its revenue rose 26% year over year to $64.6 billion. That's pretty fast among the big tech companies, but with how much Meta is spending on AI, investors want to see more. Still, this is a respectable result, and some of Meta's latest AI initiatives, such as Meta Muse, have received positive feedback and have seen heavy use. This could be a sign that Meta is headed in the right direction, and lead to better returns down the road.

Each stock is doing well in its industry, but there's still a huge piece of the puzzle missing: valuation. Sandisk is far cheaper than Meta, but that's because the market is concerned about a cyclical downturn in the industry once demand isn't as rampant.

With Sandisk growing rapidly and being priced so cheaply, I think it's the stock that I want to buy and hold right now. However, you'll have to keep a close eye on it to make sure that market conditions don't shift in the memory chip industry. If you're looking for a more set-it-and-forget-it type investment, then Meta makes more sense, as it's still in a great position to profit from the AI arms race if it continues to see success as it has in recent months.

Keithen Drury has positions in Alphabet and Meta Platforms. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Alphabet and Meta Platforms. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

During a TikTok stream where the pair were playing NBA 2K, New York Knicks guards Tyler Kolek and Miles "Deuce" McBride were asked a question: who was the "fakest" celebrity fan they encountered during the Knicks' championship run? Kolek didn't hesitate to name a major celebrity.

Kolek promptly named pop superstar Taylor Swift, who made headlines for her courtside appearance at Game 4 of the Knicks' series against the San Antonio Spurs on June 10, 2026, at Madison Square Garden. McBride teased Kolek for trying to backtrack and from the wrath of Swift's loyal fanbase.

#3104. As AI becomes more fractured, one name stands out: AMD

As Anthropic rushes to takes its shares public, the AI trade is showing cracks, and they are not confined to fringe players.

We recently wrote about CoreWeave, which fell 15.5% on Oct. 14 as yields on its 2032 notes touched 15%, and its default-swap spreads nearly doubled in October. IREN is down more than 20% this year. Last Thursday, the contagion reached chipmakers, which makes sense since much of CRWV and IREN's spending is going there. AMD dropped 8.1% as Meta's financing plans and a supply warning from Lam Research exacerbated data-center fears about the pace of AI spending.

Because when you screen for factors that demonstrably generate outperformance over time, the list narrows quickly. My screen: price above the 200-day moving average; revenue growing at least as fast as the S&P 500 (5%+ per annum); EPS growing at least as fast (7%+); rating upgrades; a PEG below 3; and ROE and ROIC of at least 12%. Of the names reporting in the next two weeks, AMD is effectively the only one that makes the list. Yes, you can (and arguably should, as our staples article described) position your portfolio with slightly less tech exposure than the broad indices provide, but we can't ignore the market's biggest and most transformative sector entirely.

Especially because the growth in this case doesn't just meet my criteria; it blows past them. Consensus for Q3 calls for EPS of $1.94 on revenue of $13.06 billion, versus $1.20 and $9.25 billion a year ago. That's YoY growth of nearly 62% and 41%, respectively. The recent drawdown came from a sector selloff, not anything AMD reported, but it shows that if some names in the space get hit, even the larger players are likely to feel it. On Oct. 6, Lisa Su said AMD would substantially increase supply in 2027 because AI orders keep outrunning capacity.

So how do you balance factors we know work for a fast-growing company against a backdrop of cracks in the AI trade? Options.

Owning the stock outright means absorbing a roughly 9% to 11% implied earnings-related move (day of). Earnings are about a week out, and over the past four quarters the smallest move over a similar window was more than 9%, and the largest move, after the company reported its Q1 26 results, was 38%! Of course, that kind of volatility means options aren't cheap, and that rich premium is also a reason not to simply buy calls.

A call spread risk reversal does both jobs: it reduces risk if the cracks widen, and the short options offset the elevated volatility we would otherwise pay for. The bottom chart shows that, by sacrificing about $1,700 of upside for $5,000 in outperformance during a severe downside move, and given how jittery this trade has been lately, this is a way to stay in it with considerably less risk. $5,000 less, specifically. Of course, selling that out will tie up some cash, but less so than simply buying the stock. And selling both the out and the call reduces long call purchase by 66%

#3100. 'The whole landscape changed': Gaming CEOs see new opportunities post-midterms

Midterm election results have created new openings for U.S. gambling expansion, while raising the prospect of greater political and legal pressure on prediction markets, according to gaming industry executives.

"The whole landscape changed," said Craig Billings, CEO of Wynn Resorts, during the company's earnings call Thursday.

Wynn has been closely watchng developments in the Middle East as it looks to open the United Arab Emirates' first legal casino in 2027. Billings said he suspects the election will have an impact on the "likely trajectory of the conflict in the region."

Closer to home, Billings sees opportunities in Texas. And he's not the only one. On the heels of reporting record third-quarter revenue and raising guidance for its brick-and-mortar business, Penn Entertainment CEO Jay Snowden called out specific opportunities made possible by state leadership changes.

Election Day was "a very good day overall for the industry, and certainly for Penn," Snowden said on Thursday's earnings call.

Texas, in particular, could be a jackpot for the casino industry. In a massive upset, Democrat Vikki Goodwin defeated longtime Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, who has been persistent in blocking gambling expansion in the Lone Star State.

"Texas is a fascinating market," Billings said, explaining how many consumers travel to Oklahoma to gamble at tribal casions. "So it's kind of a stealth market that is giant."

Penn has been building a position in Texas for years, Snowden said. It operates two of the state's three Class 1 thoroughbred racetracks and has established relationships with local leaders.

Penn plans to spend more time in Texas and, if lawmakers move toward legalization, Snowden said he expects the company is “positioned as well, if not better than really anybody in the sector.”

Las Vegas Sands also has invested heavily for many years to get casino gambling legalized in Texas.

"When Las Vegas Sands thinks about Texas and the Metroplex, it's really about an asset that will be both for business and future tourism," Sands Chairman and CEO Patrick Dumont told CNBC in an interview in October in Macao.

Dumont recently acquired the controlling stake in the Dallas Mavericks from his mother-in-law Miriam Adelson. He said there is the potential for a new Mavericks arena to incorporate a future casino.

"Whatever Las Vegas Sands can do in the future, that will be its own location, its own site and its own timeline," he said.

Houston Rockets owner Tilman Fertitta, currently serving as U.S. ambassador to Italy, owns Golden Nugget casinos, is Wynn Resorts' largest investor and is buying Caesars to take it private. Following a CNBC interview in Italy, he said, "Of course I want gaming in Texas!"

A new market would draw national sportsbook operators that would likely include DraftKings, Flutter-owned FanDuel, Caesars, Fanatics, and BetMGM, which is co-owned by MGM and Entain, among others.

Though the Texas' state election removed a major political obstacle, it didn't produce a deal. Legalizing casino gambling or sports betting would still require a constitutional amendment approved by two-thirds of both chambers and then voters.

Texas state control is now divided. While Democrats flipped the state House, Republicans kept the Senate. Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governorship.

Las Vegas Sands spokesman Ron Reese told CNBC it's too early to speculate about what might happen with Texas gaming, but that the company will monitor developments closely.

Truist gaming analyst Barry Jonas wrote in a Wednesday note that he sees mixed implications from the midterm results.

"The Ohio governor-elect Amy Acton's support for regulated online casinos could improve the chances of iGaming legalization," Jonas said. On the other hand, Nebraska voters rejected ballot measures to legalize online betting.

Georgia, where Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governorship, could also provide an opportunity. She campaigned on letting voters decide whether to legalize casino gambling, with revenue expected to be earmarked to help fund education. Sports betting and casinos remain illegal in the state, and earlier sports-betting legislation failed in the House.

Penn could also benefit if lawmakers seek tighter regulations for so-called skill-based gaming machines, which compete with casinos and licensed video gaming terminals, according to Snowden. He said candidates who support skill-based gaming machines lost seats or influence in several states.

Penn operates four casinos in Pennsylvania as well as video gaming terminals in that state and other jurisdictions, and has three casinos in Missouri.

Snowden linked recent strong year-over-year gaming revenue growth to the shutdown of skill games in Pennsylvania in mid-October. Although he cautioned that it was too early to know whether Pennsylvania’s growth would last, he noted Missouri also saw strong revenue growth as its state attorney general pursued the machines there.

In Indiana, voters in three counties rejected a proposed casino license, which Penn sees as a benefit as it limits new competition for existing casinos in Indiana and neighboring Illinois and Ohio. Some gaming insiders speculate that a wave of left-leaning progressives in power could work to limit gambling businesses.

"There's no shortage of noise about where this industry is headed, and the election certainly turns up the volume," said Joe Maloney, president of Sports Betting Alliance. "What hasn't changed with the election is what works, and that's state-regulated sports betting and iGaming, built on accountability, consumer protection, and tax revenue for states. That's our lane, and we'll make that case to every new lawmaker willing to listen."

Democratic victories are likely to increase the pressure on prediction markets, even as industry supporters call out their predictive value in forecasting the election results.

"Every eligible customer should have access to these markets, which are federally regulated through our CFTC-registered Futures Commission Merchant," a Robinhood spokesperson said.

Democrats’ control of Congress gives them subpoena power and committee resources to investigate the president’s family and business dealings. That could put Donald Trump Jr. back in the spotlight as he is a paid strategic adviser to Kalshi and sits on Polymarket’s advisory board.

Congress could also consider legislation limiting the markets’ scope. The bipartisan Prediction Markets Are Gambling Act would bar Commodity Futures Trading Commission-regulated exchanges from offering contracts based on sports or casino-style games. But the bill had only been referred to committee as of the election. A veto-proof law would require two-thirds support in both chambers; no such vote is currently scheduled.

The American Gaming Association has been fighting prediction markets as unlicensed gambling.

"The prediction markets are facing a tsunami of criminal charges, major civil investigations and significant defeats in court," Bill Miller, the trade group's CEO, told CNBC. "In the aftermath of the election, we expect the bipartisan scrutiny of these platforms to further intensify."

"Our platform is an institutional-grade exchange with strong market-integrity and customer-protection programs," Polymarket told CNBC. A spokesman said the company welcomes the opportunity to work with lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.

Repeated requests to Kalshi for comment went unanswered.

Jeff LeRiche, a partner at law firm Husch Blackwell, said he expects more scrutiny.

"Entities with robust compliance and surveillance infrastructure will be well positioned to navigate the increased attention," said LeRiche, who spent more than 20 years in the CFTC's enforcement division.

The state-level legal fight is already underway. Utah has filed criminal charges against Kalshi and its founders, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit rejected Kalshi’s request for a rehearing in its Nevada case, leaving the company exposed to state enforcement there.

New Democratic attorneys general in Ohio, Michigan and Nevada will also decide how to handle inherited disputes.

Ohio’s outgoing AG Andy Wilson helped lead a multistate effort to defend state gambling laws, Michigan’s Dana Nessel sued Kalshi and won a preliminary injunction, and Nevada’s Aaron Ford secured injunctions against prediction-market operators.

New AGs could also decide to follow Utah's lead in filing criminal charges, along with Arizona where criminal charges are pending.

#3099. Walker Kessler is having more of an impact than it looks

Since the Lakers acquired Walker Kessler over the summer, most of the conversation regarding his play, and subsequent impact, has been tied to the cost paid to land him.

The multiple years and millions of dollars, the draft picks and swaps, each have served as footnotes after every game thus far.

While fair given what the Lakers need from him going forward, it has also put increased emphasis on his raw production rather than influence. If you're into that kind of thing, Kessler's per-game numbers are solid. His 14.4 points, 10.2 rebounds and four stocks nightly will play. However, it doesn't capture the full spectrum of his impact.

On offense, Kessler is still navigating life as Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves' screener. It's an entirely new world compared to the barren guard groups he played next to with the Utah Jazz.

Things like timing, pick angles and court-mapping will take time. But the early results have been encouraging nevertheless.

After his dunk-centric eruption on opening night, defenses have already begun selling out in the paint to take away his lob and cut chances.

Due to this, Kessler has not been able to duplicate his scoring outbursts, but it hasn't lessened his value to the offense either. A direct result of teams loading up and tagging Kessler — often with multiple defenders — is that it has created open shots from the perimeter, as seen in the clips below.

Kessler's roll gravity also extends to his rebounding ability. As one of the league's best second-chance creators, and simply being a massive person, Kessler often draws multiple players to him whenever a shot goes up.

This fear is well warranted. The Lakers' offensive rebound percentage jolts up nearly 10% when Kessler is on the floor compared to off. Like a black hole, this sucks up defenders from the corners and creates quality looks for shooters. The Lakers are currently shooting 43.9% from the corners this season, the second-best mark in the league.

Beyond the attention Kessler attracts on offense simply from existing, his omnipresence is probably best demonstrated with the impact he's had on the Lakers' defense.

As the backbone and backline, Kessler's presence in the paint has allowed the team's wings to be extremely aggressive shocking the ball with the trust that the center will clean up any mistakes. This disruptive style has resulted in the Lakers being one of the best defenses in terms of forced turnovers.

And when his teammates do get burned for gambling or getting blown by, Kessler has been iron-clad protecting the basket.

Not only are opposing teams shooting just 26.9% of their shots at the rim when Kessler is on the floor — would rank fourth-best in the NBA — they are also missing once he meets them there.

Among the 12 players who have defended at least 50 shots within six feet this season, Kessler ranks first in defended shooting percentage against (45.1%) while also contesting the second-most attempts behind only Victor Wembanyama, according to the league's tracking data.

Kessler's deterrence and effectiveness in shutting off the paint is not solely due to his size.

His height and frightening wingspan do help, yes. But what drives his success is his impressive motor. With every second jump contest, race down the floor and closeout to a 3-point shooter, Kessler's care factor is never in doubt. That goes a long way to actualizing his defensive upside.

Despite how hard he ultimately tries, the Lakers are learning firsthand that Kessler can't be everywhere at once. This is never more true than the defensive drop-off once he's on the bench.

Through their first nine games, the Lakers have allowed a defensive rating of 110.1 with Kessler on the court compared to 117.2 when he's been off. That's a discrepancy that is the equivalent of the team performing like the eighth-best defense versus the 26th.

While his individual numbers will likely fluctuate nightly, and even quarterly, as illustrated by his dominant final frame — 10 points, five rebounds, four blocks and a steal — against the Sacramento Kings on Wednesday, Kessler has proven to be more than suited for the role bestowed upon him.

He may not be the thundering force that Dončić is or as crafty as Reaves, but Kessler's job as the Lakers' silent protector has been as critical to the team's strong start.

It won't always look like he's had a good game in the box score. But just watch how that opposing ball-handler goes wide-eyed and makes a U-turn when the giant in purple and gold makes his stand.

More than any numbers can ever quantify, Kessler's game is measured in fear. And the Lakers are benefiting from it so far.

All stats courtesy of Cleaning the Glass unless otherwise stated. You can follow Alex on Bluesky at @alexregla.bsky.social

#3097. Family offices boost startup investments in October, backing women's health and caregivers

A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.

After a slow September, investment firms of ultra-wealthy families stepped up their deal-making last month. In October, family offices made 56 direct investments in companies, up about 30% from the month prior, according to data provided exclusively to CNBC by Fintrx, a private wealth intelligence platform.

Laurene Powell Jobs' Emerson Collective was the most prolific investor of the month, backing three healthcare startups according to Fintrx data. Her investment and philanthropy firm seeks to address health equity and other complex challenges like the energy transition.

Last month, Emerson Collective joined a $555 million Series G for Devoted Health, a healthcare provider and insurer of Medicare Advantage plans, alongside information technology billionaire Azim Premji's namesake family office. Devoted Health, which has counted Emerson Collective as an investor since 2021, announced that it will use the fundraise to expand to five additional states for a total of 34.

Powell Jobs' firm also participated in two fundraises for healthcare data startups BioStack and Collective X Health. BioStack, which raised $9.5 million in seed funding, analyzes patient records across different institutions to create training datasets for artificial intelligence healthcare models. Collective X Health, fresh off a $3.2 million pre-seed round, seeks to close the gender data gap by compiling and licensing peer-reviewed, female-specific data and research.

Emerson Collective is in good company as family offices continue to invest in healthcare innovations from telehealth to drug discovery. In a family office survey released by Citi Wealth in September, healthcare ranked as the second-most-popular sector for direct investing at 32%, only behind AI at 51%.

Melinda French Gates' Pivotal Ventures joined an $82 million Series C for Abby Care, an AI-enabled startup that trains and certifies family members as paid caregivers under Medicaid and Medicare programs.

Erin Harkless Moore, who manages investments at Pivotal Ventures, told CNBC that the firm looks for founders who have first-hand experience with the complexities of healthcare. Abby Care CEO and founder Havi Nguyen started navigating the Medicaid system at age 9 as a caregiver for her sisters and eventually her grandparents.

"We look for teams that understand the problem deeply and have a model built for the realities of the healthcare system as it currently exists. Abby Care is a great example," Moore said. "Their deep understanding of the market allowed them to both spot an unsolved problem and understand how to navigate the regulatory challenges in this space."

For family offices looking to invest in healthcare, Moore said overlooked markets offer a chance to back companies addressing needs that have long gone unmet.

"Women's health is a space that has been historically underfunded and under-researched. We have less data, less funding, and huge gaps to fill," she said. "That can make investing more challenging, but it can also point to where there's real opportunity."

The Inside Wealth newsletter by Robert Frank is your weekly guide to high-net-worth investors and the industries that serve them.

#3094. Ripple strikes deal with Robinhood to expand its RLUSD digital dollar

Ripple has struck a deal with Robinhood to expand the reach of its digital dollar, RLUSD, strengthening trading and financing links between their institutional businesses and improving Robinhood's internal money management.

The partnership involves using RLUSD to settle institutional trades, automate Robinhood's treasury operations and expand access to digital asset trading and financing through Ripple Prime and Bitstamp, the global crypto exchange acquired by Robinhood last year.

It also helps meet Robinhood's ambition of becoming a global financial superapp, centralizing its customers' financial lives while expanding the underlying infrastructure that can serve both retail and institutional clients.

"Utility is what moves stablecoins forward. Working with Ripple, Bitstamp and Robinhood will have access to RLUSD for institutional settlement, Ripple Treasury for our operations and Ripple Prime for financing," Robinhood Crypto General Manager Johann Kerbrat said in a statement shared with CNBC. "That is what a connected, global financial system looks like."

Stablecoins have long been a workhorse of the crypto world, giving traders a way to move money among exchanges, buy and sell crypto assets, and park funds between trades without having to convert back into traditional currency. But as the crypto industry evolves beyond trading and markets move toward 24/7 liquidity, stablecoins are becoming essential financial infrastructure because of their ability to enable near-instant settlement and move dollar-denominated value at any time, regardless of traditional banking hours.

As firms look to do more with stablecoins beyond simply listing them on exchanges, stablecoin issuers are betting they'll favor a one-stop-shop approach that bundles the technology and services needed to move money, settle trades and manage cash.

"Stablecoins have evolved from a crypto trading tool into a critical piece of financial infrastructure," Ripple President Monica Long told CNBC. "The clearest evidence of this is where they're now being embedded — from corporate payments to capital markets. Our partnership with Robinhood reflects that evolution."

"This is about much more than trading," she added. "It's about fundamentally changing how money moves and is managed — giving institutions the ability to operate 24/7/365, unlocking liquidity and putting capital to work more efficiently."

Circle Internet Group, a Ripple competitor, is positioning itself for a similar future, where winning platforms, in addition to issuing stablecoins, also provide the infrastructure to put them to work. Earlier this year, for example, it launched the Circle Payments Network, connecting financial institutions and payment providers using its flagship USDC stablecoin and other digital assets for cross-border payments.

The network is Circle's answer to the 8-year-old Ripple Payments business, a service that helps businesses move money across borders, using any of several assets moving through that system, including USDC, Ripple-created XRP and, as of its debut in December 2024, RLUSD.

RLUSD's market cap has grown to more than $2.5 billion. Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC still dominate the total stablecoin market, which now exceeds $300 billion.

RLUSD will also be listed on Robinhood's trading platform, and is currently available to traders on Bitstamp as well as Robinhood Chain, the company's home-grown blockchain for tokenized stocks and other assets.

Robinhood, which reports third-quarter results for the three months ended in September after the market closes, rose about 2.5% in early trading Tuesday, snapping a three-day decline.

Correction: A previous headline misspelled RLUSD.
